Why does the Tathāgata refer to a bodhisattva mahāsattva as a *srotāpanna*?
Ānanda, you should know this!"
The inconceivable Buddha-way is called *srotāpanna*.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in non-dwelling, they draw near to the Buddha-way; they do not grasp at any phenomena, have nothing upon which to rely, and no object of perception;
they do not abide in any phenomena, for they are ultimately unarisen.
In order to attain this path, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices firm diligence and firm contemplation without indolence;

he never opposes it and his mind has no dependence. Regarding the unsurpassed, most supreme, and essential path traversed by all Buddhas, he neither clings to this path nor dwells within it, yet he seeks all dharmas through such a path.
Although he seeks them, he finds nothing to be attained, and thus he neither moves nor dwells within that path.

One can give rise to equanimity regarding the perception of the path, the perception of birth-and-death, and the perception of the Buddha; one attains equanimity regarding the phenomena that constitute fetters and hindrances, the equanimity of all phenomena, and the equanimity of all Buddhas. Having distanced oneself from the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one can give rise to the vision of the Buddha and awaken from all views. Having cultivated the perception of remedies, one has already transcended the perception of a self (*ātman*).
Ānanda! For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is called a srotāpanna.

They do not cling to the Buddha-way, having attained the undefiled way; they have no doubt regarding the Buddha’s bodhi; they do not select precepts, even to the point of not perceiving the Buddha’s precepts.

Because they do not perceive [a self], they do not select or discriminate regarding the precepts; they have forever severed the three fetters and do not dwell within the triple world. Having attained the Buddha-way, they are free from the notion of sentient beings; having no place of reliance, they are detached from the phenomena of reliance, seeking exclusively for the Buddha-way and attaining the path of peace and tranquility.
Not sparing even their own bodies or lives, they are able to relinquish all things with a joyful heart; their countenances are harmonious and pleasant, free from any frown or wrinkle.
For the sake of Bodhi, they practice giving, such that there is no small thing they cannot renounce.

To rescue suffering sentient beings, to lead them to Nirvana, to cultivate the dharmas with signs, and to attain the signless dharma, they leave behind the notion of a "sentient being" and enter into the fearlessness of the multitude, preaching the dharma of tranquility to purify the path to Bodhi.
They are free from all fear, even unto the fear of death.

Why is this? Because they have attained the Dharma of tranquility, are far removed from dust and defilement, abide securely in the Buddha-way, and have skillfully cultivated the path of non-conceptualization—the equanimity toward all realms of miserable rebirth.
"Ānanda! For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is called a srotāpanna.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The inconceivable Buddha-way is called *srotāpanna*;
if one abides in this way, one will surely flow into bodhi.
This way is like space; it does not rely on any phenomena.”
Without conditions and without abiding, all that exists cannot be apprehended.
The Bodhisattva, through firm and diligent effort, is able to attain such a Dharma;
it is the unsurpassed, supreme path of deliverance taught by the Buddhas who guide the world.
One does not become attached to this path, nor does one dwell within it;
by seeking through this path, one does not perceive any phenomena.
This path is without movement, and likewise without dwelling within.
Unwearied like the Buddha, without opposition and free from fear;
regarding the characteristics of birth and death as he does the perception of the Buddha—
being able to maintain such equanimity, know that one is a *srotāpanna*.
All fetters and hindrances that can obscure the Buddha-way are entirely able to be left far behind; this is called a Srotāpanna.
One who is able to sever the view of a self-body and give rise to the vision of the Buddha—
Having awakened from all false views, one skillfully cultivates the perception of their antidotes;
skillfully cultivating the perception of the self, one knows the faults of the notion of "I.
This is called a *srotāpanna*, who does not cling even to the Buddha-way.
Even if one should give rise to this doubt,
"I shall not attain bodhi," one immediately attains freedom from defilement and seeks the Buddha-way.
One does not discriminate regarding the precepts, nor does one harbor a desire for the Buddha's śīla.
Having already severed the notion of precepts, they do not discriminate regarding the *śīla*.
Having forever severed the three fetters, they do not dwell within the triple world;
having already attained the Buddha-way, they skillfully cultivate the perception of sentient beings.
Seeking awakening through a path that has no object of perception,
one attains the Buddha’s stainless awakening, the path of ultimate tranquility;
delighting in the practice of giving, with a serene countenance free from frowning.
Not sparing even one's own body or life, for the sake of the path free from conceptual proliferation;
for the sake of suffering sentient beings, one is able to relinquish everything;
causing them to transcend the stage of Srotāpanna and reach the most wondrous and supreme fruit.
Distant from all notions of existence, They have skillfully mastered signlessness;
For this reason, they are free from Ill repute and all fears.
Regarding what is taught as Dharma or non-Dharma, They are able to remain detached from both.
Remaining unstained by them within, one has no fear of ill repute.
When entering a great assembly, the mind is free from fear;
proclaiming the Dharma of cessation, one has already purified the path to enlightenment.
If one gives rise to the perception of sentient beings, one can produce their true reality;
for this reason, being stainless, one is far removed from all fear.
Having already abandoned all terrors, one reaches the state where there is nothing to fear.
Having attained the path of tranquility, secure and unsurpassed;
knowing the equality of the miserable realms, one gives rise to no fear;
when this path manifests before one, there is no notion of a self.
The Bodhisattva, through such a teaching, is called a *srotāpanna*;
for the sake of those who delight in inferior teachings, he speaks in this way.
By means of subtle and wondrous skillful means, he proclaims the Buddha-dharma.
For those who are heedless on the path, the Guides,
the Buddhas, have taught such a Dharma by relinquishing [other] skillful means;
it is for those who have long practiced and who seek the most supreme path.
For this reason, Ānanda!
I speak of the srotāpanna;
those sentient beings who possess wisdom are able to understand this matter.
For this reason, Ānanda,
I speak of the srotāpanna;
those beings who lack wisdom falsely discriminate regarding this matter.
Those with small and ignorant minds do not understand the subtle and esoteric speech;
with deluded hearts they give rise to disputes and fail to comprehend the profound meaning.
Only when one has fulfilled the many hundreds of dharmas is one called a Srotāpanna.
"By means of the name 'srotāpanna,' the qualities of all Buddhas are revealed.
In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgatas,
the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, through the power of skillful means, speak of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas as being 'srotāpannas' for the sake of the śrāvakas."
The Sūtra of Vast, Majestic, and Pure [Vows], Scroll Two.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Vast, Majestic, and Pure Non-retrogressive Wheel,
Scroll Three.
Furthermore, Ānanda, why does the Tathāgata call a bodhisattva mahāsattva a sakṛdāgāmin?
Ānanda, you should know this!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, following and studying the Buddha’s wisdom, understands that awakening does not arise from conditions; for the sake of non-conditioned wisdom, they seek the Buddha’s wisdom.

Through various causes and conditions, they seek a meditative concentration that has no fixed location, thereby seeking the Buddha’s wisdom to incinerate the dharmas of affliction. By incinerating all afflictions, they attain the Buddha’s dharma of equality, seeking the unattained dharma such as that of the Buddhas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Although he delivers sentient beings, he does not stir the seeking of sentient beings, nor does he stir the realm of sentient beings.

There are sentient beings whose wisdom and minds are feeble, who are distressed by sorrow and affliction, and who do not understand the Dharma-realm; desiring to cause these multitudes to abide in wisdom, he seeks the Buddha-wisdom. Regarding the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path, liberations, and samādhis, he first awakens himself and then awakens sentient beings, seeking the Buddha-wisdom through which the wisdom that can reach the site of enlightenment may be attained.
In order to attain this wisdom, one seeks the Buddha-wisdom and the Buddha-eye—that inconceivable, unobstructed eye—constantly using this eye to benefit the world.

In order to seek this eye of wisdom—that supreme wisdom among all wisdoms which is the wisdom to be employed—and because one knows that all phenomena are suchness and yet unattainable, and because this wisdom is the wisdom to be employed to cause all sentient beings to abide within it—namely, the wisdom of non-abiding in any phenomenon—for these reasons, I have come to this place.
Having arrived, one sees the realm of sentient beings; this is an inconceivable realm. Having sought this realm, one does not find it—whence, then, do sentient beings arise?
One does not know the places where sentient beings are born.

While there are distinct names for the realm of sentient beings, when one contemplates the dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings, one does not perceive any marks of distinction. One sees that the realm of sentient beings entirely enters the dharma-realm; one sees that the dharma-realm is the path of equality, the path of the Buddha-dharma, the path wherein sentient beings cannot be apprehended, and the path of the wisdom of the equality of sentient beings.

For the sake of seeking this incomparable wisdom, this wisdom is pure and free from dust and defilement; one cannot attain this wisdom by means of this wisdom, for one knows that this wisdom is a wisdom in which there is nothing to be known.
It is because of this wisdom that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess distinctions; not yet having attained this wisdom, they come to this realm in order to seek it. Ānanda!
"For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is called a sakṛdāgāmin.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Following and learning the wisdom of all Buddhas, That wisdom is unsurpassed; Thus, he returns but once more to this world."
Because they seek the wisdom of the Buddha, they are called Sakṛdāgāmins.
The various causes and conditions they have explained can give rise to Bodhi;
for such reasons as these, they have come to this world.
The dhyāna of nowhere spoken of can burn away all afflictions;
for this reason I have come here, in order to give birth to this dhyāna.
It is a dharma never before attained, the sphere of activity of the All-Knowing One.
Because I also wish to seek [the truth], I have come to this place.
All sentient beings are immovable, and the dharma-realm is likewise;
because it is not to be moved, I have therefore come to this place.
Suffering and lacking wisdom, all sentient beings are filled with grief and anxiety;
wishing to cause such multitudes to dwell in the Buddha’s immeasurable wisdom—
[I shall establish them] in the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, the path, liberation, and meditative concentration.
To awaken oneself and to awaken others, one seeks the wisdom of the Buddhas.
Being able to proceed toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
the dharma practiced by the Buddhas of the past— for the sake of seeking this dharma, I have come to this place.
Seeking such wisdom, the inconceivable Buddha-eye;
for the sake of seeking such an eye, I have come to this world.
This is the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas, the Teachers who guide the world.
Seeking such wisdom, the most supreme among all forms of knowledge—
the wisdom by which one can know the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena—
this wisdom is unattainable; how then can one seek all phenomena?
I vow to cause many sentient beings to dwell securely in unsurpassed wisdom;
desiring also to let others know this, I have come to this world.
Having arrived and beheld sentient beings, I see that their realms are inconceivable.
Therefore, the Sakṛdāgāmin comes here seeking sentient beings;
yet, in seeking the realm of sentient beings, no sentient being can be found.
Thus, although he comes seeking, he likewise cannot be known.
They do not know sentient beings, nor the realm of sentient beings;
yet if they can know this realm, they know the distinctions among sentient beings.
They observe all phenomena, and having observed them, they see nothing at all.
Abiding in a concentrated mind, one seeks all the Buddha-dharmas.
If one possesses this pure wisdom, its stainless nature is pristine;
yet even while not grasping at this wisdom, one knows that which is to be known.
Because such sentient beings are able to attain this wisdom, they are called "Bodhisattvas Without Dependence"; for this reason, they have come to this world. Ānanda!
For this reason, one is called a Sakṛdāgāmin;
sentient beings lacking wisdom mistakenly discriminate regarding this matter. Ānanda!
For these reasons, one is called a Sakṛdāgāmin;
only those beings who are diligent and energetic can understand this matter.
The wise comprehend the subtle and esoteric, reaching certainty regarding the profound Dharma.
One who can understand such meanings will swiftly give rise to bodhi.
"It is thus, Ānanda!
By the power of skillful means, the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, speaks of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva for the sake of śrāvakas, calling him a sakṛdāgāmin."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
Why does the Tathāgata call a bodhisattva mahāsattva an *anāgāmin*?
Ānanda, you should know this!"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has already transcended the conduct of ordinary beings and attained the conduct of the Buddhas; having distanced himself from all dharmas of conditioned activity, he knows that dharmas neither come nor go. Within all dharmas, he has no reliance and no dwelling; therefore, he does not come to this world.
Why is this? It is because one does not perceive any characteristic of coming or going in phenomena.

Having transcended ordinary beings and abandoned the notion of being an ordinary being, and having also transcended the notion of a Buddha, one dwells in no phenomenon whatsoever; there are no causes or conditions that can cause anything to come.
Why is this? Because they have already attained the realm of tranquility.

The Buddhas, the guides of the world, declare that ordinary persons do not attain rebirth through dhyāna; for such practitioners have departed from all places of difficulty, have eternally severed craving and desire, do not covet solid food, have forever abandoned the perception of food, have attained awakening, and demonstrate to all those with false views that there is nothing to which one should cling.

Knowing that the nature of the sixty-two views is identical to nirvana, one is free from the perception of hindrances; being free from all faults and afflictions within all phenomena, one is pure and stainless, subduing arrogance and extracting the arrow of ignorance.

Having already destroyed the fetter of craving, they no longer experience delight or attachment; having incinerated all afflictions, they are free from all conceptualizations; having extracted the arrows of sorrow and distress, they are liberated from pride and arrogance; being well-versed in all sounds, they attain illuminating wisdom; riding upon the inconceivable Buddha-vehicle, they realize the nature of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

Having left behind the mire of desire, one attains the treasury hidden by former Buddhas—the supreme treasury of wisdom, which neither increases nor decreases—and thereby obtains the Buddha-vehicle, the most exalted among all vehicles for sentient beings.

Free from the perceptions of existence and non-existence and having severed all doubts, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes such dharmas as these does not return to this realm; he is called an anāgāmin.
Furthermore, Ānanda,
there are sentient beings with whom bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have a connection, whom they cause to abide in bodhi.
How do they cause them to abide?
What are called sentient beings are themselves bodhi, and bodhi is itself sentient beings; one is able to awaken to the notion of sentient beings.
Why is this? Because one has already fully realized that their nature is empty.

Because they know that the realm of sentient beings is an inconceivable realm, they are able to awaken to this perception and know that the realm of sentient beings is itself the realm of empty space. Since the realm of empty space is empty, it is far removed from the realm of sentient beings; the realm of empty space does not abide anywhere apart from the nature of emptiness, for the realm of empty space is empty by its very nature of emptiness. By means of such dharmas, they cause all sentient beings to dedicate themselves toward Bodhi.
Why is this? Because one knows that sentient beings are the realm of empty space;
the realm of sentient beings entirely enters the realm of empty space.
Why is this so? Because the nature of sentient beings and the nature of all phenomena each enter into one another. Why is this so?
Because they cannot be apprehended.
Because they cannot be apprehended, they do not come to this world; for this reason, they are called *anāgāmin* (Non-returners).
Among all dharmas, there is no characteristic of number, and the Buddhas have already transcended the characteristics of number.
"Ānanda! For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is called an anāgāmin.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Having departed, they do not return; they no longer cultivate the practice of going.
Because they have already abandoned the practice of going, they are called Anāgāmins.
Well-knowing the characteristics of coming and going, they do not rely on any phenomena."
Having no further place to go, they cannot return to this world.
The Buddhas, the guides and teachers of the world, have taught the dhyāna of ordinary persons;
because they do not go back to that realm again, they are called Anāgāmins.
All phenomena have no characteristic of coming, and the characteristic of going cannot be found;
having attained the state where there is neither coming nor going, this is called an Anāgāmin.
Such a person shall never again proceed toward the three evil realms.
Having attained all Buddha-dharmas, this is called an Anāgāmin;
having forever severed all desire and not craving for solid food,
having attained the path of Bodhi, this is called an Anāgāmin.
The various bases of views that have been taught number sixty-two;
because he no longer dwells in these bases of views, he is called an Anāgāmin.
All dharmas lack intrinsic nature and characteristics; he has already departed from intrinsic nature and characteristics.
Because they have understood reality as it is, they will not return to this world again.
They proclaim the tranquility of nirvāṇa, which can incinerate all afflictions;
because they have distanced themselves from all signs, they do not return to this world.
Having severed all states of difficulty, Able to remain far removed from dust and defilement;
Having reached the secure state of Nirvāṇa, This is called an Anāgāmin.
Having already subdued the Evil Māra And all his retinue;
Unmoved by those things, he is called an Anāgāmin.
Having extracted the arrow of ignorance and severed all fetters of craving;
having fully awakened to the nature of sensual desire, he is called an Anāgāmin.
Able to incinerate all afflictions, And likewise free from all notions of existence;
Possessing the certain, supreme, and wondrous fruit— This is called an Anāgāmin.
Having already extracted the arrows of sorrow and distress, And having eliminated all forms of pride and arrogance;
One who well understands the characteristics of the five aggregates is called an Anāgāmin.
Having attained all illuminations and the inconceivable Buddha-vehicle,
and having distanced oneself from the mire of desire, one is called an Anāgāmin.
Having attained the treasury of great wisdom, the treasury preserved by the Buddhas of the past;
the most excellent among all treasuries—this is called an Anāgāmin.
Having already established themselves in the unsurpassed Great Vehicle of all Buddhas.
Having forever severed all doubting minds, they are called Anāgāmins.
Causing all sentient beings with whom they have a connection to abide in Bodhi;
for the sake of those who abide in Bodhi, they do not return to this world.
One who can know all the realms of emptiness, And that the realm of sentient beings is inconceivable;
Having already abandoned such conceptualizations— This one is called an Anāgāmin.
One who can know the realm of sentient beings And that the dharma-realm is empty;
Not perceiving any sentient beings—this is called an Anāgāmin.
Their minds no longer seek to grasp at the signs of existence;
having reached the state of signlessness, this is called an Anāgāmin.
Ānanda! By virtue of this matter, one is called an Anāgāmin;
by means of the dharma of non-abiding, one dwells within the Buddha-dharma.
"Therefore, Ānanda!
By the power of skillful means, the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, speaks of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva as being an Anāgāmin for the sake of the Śrāvakas."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
Why does the Tathāgata refer to a bodhisattva mahāsattva as an arhat?
Ānanda, you should know this!"

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, having departed from all practices of the [śrāvaka] levels, should practice the conduct of a Buddha; they should perform the work of rescuing all sentient beings by destroying their afflictions. They should untie the bonds of affliction for those sentient beings who suffer from them, yet they neither apprehend a sentient being nor apprehend the bonds of affliction. One who should perform such deeds is called an arhat.

Having relinquished abiding in that which exists, one dwells in non-attainment; knowing all things are empty, and knowing that this emptiness is also empty, one penetrates signlessness. By being free from all signs and abandoning all conceptualizations, one recognizes that the conceptualization of sentient beings is a dharma of affliction. Being able to relinquish ignorance and realize the dharma of no-mind, one clearly understands the dharma of emptiness and should attain bodhi. One should give rise to the inconceivable Buddha-bodhi; for these reasons, one is called an Arhat.

One should proclaim the Dharma as the Buddhas of the three periods have taught, are teaching, and will teach; for that which is taught is entirely quiescent, free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), pure and stainless. Because one has thoroughly realized this matter, one is called an Arhat.

One should cause sentient beings to abide in bodhi, knowing that all dharmas and bodhi itself are non-existent and ungraspable. One should cultivate the compassion of a Buddha rather than the compassion for sentient beings; with such compassion, one universally takes sentient beings as an object of focus, yet does not apprehend a "sentient being. Having attained this compassion in which sentient beings are unapprehendable, one is therefore called an Arhat.

One should teach that all dharmas benefit sentient beings, yet without giving rise to the conceptualization of "dharma" or "non-dharma"; among all dharmas, one should always take precedence—this is called an Arhat.

One should preach the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and the path for the sake of sentient beings, yet remain unstained by and unattached to these dharmas; therefore, one is called an Arhat.
One should cause sentient beings to know pure bodhi and cause those sentient beings to give rise to such bodhi; therefore, one is called an Arhat.

One should not be greedily attached to the gains and offerings of sentient beings in the world; one should preach to sentient beings the Dharma of non-attachment to gain and offerings. Because one preaches this Dharma, one is called an Arhat.
One should go to the worlds of all Buddhas and see all Buddhas as a Buddha sees a Buddha; having seen such Buddha-worlds,
one should resolve the mind to seek such worlds— namely, the inconceivable world,
the immeasurable world, the unequaled world, and the boundless world.
The world without conceptual proliferation, the world that is ineffable, the world of emptiness, the world of signlessness,
the world of wishlessness, the world of non-retrogression, the world free from women, the world free from sexual desire,
the world without afflictions, the world of the Buddha’s unimpeded eloquence, and the world of the bodhisattvas.

Regarding realms: the realm without obstruction, the realm without defilement, the realm that subdues Māra, the realm without enemies, and the realm where there is no final nirvāṇa—among all such worlds, these are supreme;
one should seek such worlds, and for this reason, one is called an Arhat.
Because he should give rise to all dharmas that have not yet arisen, he is called an Arhat.
Because he is unstained by desire and does not give rise to anger toward things that provoke it, he is called an Arhat.
Because they swiftly and thoroughly penetrate the supreme knowledge of the cessation of the origin [of suffering], they are called Arhats.
Because they are Arhats, they are called Bodhi; because they are Bodhi, they are called Arhats.

Enlightenment is immovable because the realm of sentient beings is immovable; one should cause hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings to abide in the path of enlightenment, and because they abide in the path of enlightenment, they are called Arhats.

All sentient beings and awakening arise from non-discrimination; one should teach all sentient beings this dharma of equality. This dharma of equality has no equal among all dharmas; this equal awakening arises from non-discrimination. One should know such a dharma, and having known this dharma, one explains it to sentient beings without increase or decrease. Because one accomplishes the dharma of non-increase and non-decrease, one is called an Arhat.
One should explain that such a one is called an Arhat because they have departed from sounds and dharmas.
One should understand that such a one is free from the attachments of many sentient beings— namely, the attachment to the unobtainability of sentient beings,

the attachment to the views of annihilationism and eternalism regarding sentient beings, the attachment to the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) regarding sentient beings, and the attachment to being unable to transcend [suffering]— and they perceive all dharmas as non-arising.

They do not cling to the unconditioned, the uncreated, or the unextinguished; they do not destroy their clinging to form, nor do they destroy their clinging to feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness.
They leave behind clinging to the dharmas of ordinary worldlings, yet they establish clinging to the dharmas of the Buddhas.

They maintain clinging to the notion of the fruit of stream-entry, clinging to the notion of the fruit of once-returning, clinging to the notion of the fruit of non-returning, and clinging to the fruit of arhatship.
They dwell on the thought of the fruit of a śrāvaka; they dwell on the thought of the fruit of a pratyekabuddha;

they dwell on the thought of the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; they dwell on the thought of bodhicitta; for the sake of bodhi, they dwell on attachment while practicing giving; for the sake of bodhi, they dwell on attachment while guarding the precepts;
they dwell on attachment while practicing patience by grasping at the thought of anger; they dwell on attachment while practicing diligence by grasping at the thought of indolence; they grasp at...
They are attached to the arising of meditative concentration from distracted thoughts; they are attached to cultivating wisdom through the grasping of unwholesome views;
they are attached to parents, wives, children, male and female relatives, brothers, sisters, and all beloved kin; they are attached to the desire to see and cherish their loved ones;
they are attached to delighting in idle talk; and they are attached to the dualistic view that treats the phenomena of affliction and the phenomena of liberation as two separate things.

Attachment to gain and offerings; attachment to seeing those who are householders or those who have left the home life; attachment to seeing inferior or superior dharmas; attachment to being separated from the dharmas of ordinary beings;
attachment to taking the Buddha-dharmas as a condition; attachment to seeing lower or higher dharmas; attachment to the skillful means of possessing all marks;
and attachment to conceiving notions regarding the world of Buddhas—because one should eliminate such attachments of sentient beings, it is called "A" (Arhat).

An Arhat does not discriminate between those who are sentient beings and those who are the dharma of nirvāṇa; nor between those who are sentient beings and those who are not the dharma of nirvāṇa; nor between those who can produce dharmas and those who cannot produce dharmas; nor between those who practice bodhi and those who cannot practice bodhi; nor between those who uphold the precepts and those who violate the precepts; nor between those who possess much merit and those who possess little merit. One who does not give rise to such dualistic views is called an Arhat.

Furthermore, they do not discriminate between sentient beings who are fields of merit and those who are not; they do not discriminate between sentient beings who are diligent and those who are not; they do not discriminate between sentient beings who are ordinary and inferior and those whose wisdom is clear; nor do they give rise to such dualistic views as "this is a woman," "this is a man," "this is neither male nor female," "this is the Dharma," or "this is not the Dharma. One who does not give rise to such dualistic views is called an Arhat.

Furthermore, they do not discriminate by thinking, "This being is regressing from enlightenment," or "This being is not regressing from enlightenment"; "This being has attained mastery over enlightenment," or "This being has not attained mastery over enlightenment"; "This being is near to enlightenment," or "This being is far from enlightenment. They do not give rise to such thoughts as, "I shall attain enlightenment and enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder. In brief, because they are able to eliminate all attachments of sentient beings, they are called *arhats*.

Ānanda! Having thus removed the attachments of sentient beings, the Arhat also explains the true nature of sentient beings for them; because he teaches such a Dharma, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is called an Arhat.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Having already been able to relinquish all The various practices of the stages;
Because he can relinquish these practices, He is named an Arhat.”
Able to sever all afflictions and the fetters of suffering sentient beings,
causing them all to attain liberation— this is called an Arhat.
Far removed from anything obtainable, they abide in the dharma of non-attainment.
Knowing that all phenomena are empty is called an arhat.
Having already understood and realized emptiness, they also penetrate signlessness;
being far removed from all signs, this is called an arhat.
One should practice the most supreme conduct, that which all Buddhas have practiced;
deliver all sentient beings from the great perils of birth and death.
Having already abandoned all marks, one knows that the perceptions of sentient beings are illusory.
Because they are able to relinquish all conceptualizations, they are called Arhats.
Having relinquished all notions of ignorance and attained mastery over the mindless dharma,
and because they have realized the dharma of emptiness, they are called Arhats.
One should attain the inconceivable awakening of all Buddhas;
one should practice with diligent vigor—this is called an Arhat.
One should proclaim all dharmas as pure and free from conceptual proliferation.
Causing sentient beings to abide in the Path—this is called an Arhat.
One should employ universal compassion to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings;
yet, not apprehending a "sentient being"—this is called an Arhat.
One should proclaim all dharmas as supreme among the multitudes;
having no notion of "dharma" or "non-dharma," such a person is called an Arhat.
For the sake of all sentient beings, one should teach the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path.
One who is unstained by and unattached to these phenomena is called an Arhat.
One who should cause other sentient beings to awaken to and realize the pure Dharma,
and who is likewise able to give rise to Bodhi, is called an Arhat.
One should not give rise to greedy attachment toward any worldly gain or offerings;
because one does not crave such gain and offerings, one is called an Arhat.
One should go to visit the Buddhas in the adorned, pure, and wondrous worlds.
Wherever the Buddhas dwell, they preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
One should give rise to this mind and seek this adorned and pure realm;
because one seeks this realm, such a person is called an Arhat.
Untainted by desire, not giving rise to anger where there is cause for it;
knowing that awakening is equal—this is called an Arhat.
Having attained knowledge of cessation and its origination, they have thoroughly realized the mark of tranquility.
Because of the path to enlightenment, he is called an Arhat.
Within the realms of all sentient beings, he does not move any being;
yet he causes many billions of beings to all abide upon the path to enlightenment.
Sentient beings and bodhi arise from non-discrimination;
one who can know this equality is called an arhat.
Among all dharmas that are equal, this dharma of equality is the most supreme.
These and awakening arise from non-conceptualization.
Having realized this, one teaches it to others without increase or decrease;
since they also arise from this Dharma, they are called Arhats.
For the sake of these sentient beings, one should preach the Dharma that is without sound;
thus liberating many beings, yet there is no one who moves.
Sentient beings cannot be apprehended, nor can the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
To eliminate all false views and enable liberation from manifold sufferings,
[one must realize that] all phenomena are characterized by arising and ceasing, yet are ultimately unconditioned and without activity;
yet sentient beings, afflicted by various pains and distresses, discriminate them according to their marks.
Not destroying form, and likewise with feeling;
with perception, volitional formations, and consciousness—cause them to be free from these attachments.
Within these dharmas of ordinary beings, one perceives movement.
Abiding in the Buddha-dharma without abiding, they cause all to attain liberation.
Abiding in the notion of various fruits, and likewise in the notion of a pratyekabuddha,
they preach the Dharma for sentient beings, causing them to abandon the attachment to the notion of a Buddha.
Attached to the bodhicitta, and likewise attached to giving;
attached to precepts and patience—for them he teaches the Dharma of non-attachment.
Grasping at the notion of indolence, they engage in the practice of diligence through conceptualization.
Concentrated mind and distracted thought, Evil wisdom and sublime wisdom— Not discriminating between these phenomena, Knowing them to be devoid of manifold characteristics;
One should speak thus: Such a person is named an Arhat.
Firmly clinging to the notion of a self, śrāvakas engage in much conceptual discrimination;
to eliminate such discrimination, one should preach the Dharma for them.
Parents, wives, and children—due to a lack of wisdom, they are greedily attached to these.
This path is not enlightenment; it is the domain of birth and death.
These are my brothers, and these sisters are objects of my affectionate thoughts.
One who has eliminated that craving and attachment is called an Arhat.
Thus they employ clever speech to incite the hearts of others toward joy and courage;
desiring to see former acquaintances and kin,
when the time comes for them to meet, they develop mutual attachment and craving.
Due to ignorance and perversion, one belongs to Māra and lacks self-mastery.
Remaining far removed from all gain and offerings, and knowing the faults and afflictions inherent in such gain,
one should, for the sake of all sentient beings, speak of the faults of gain and offerings.
"This is the dharma of affliction; this is the dharma of liberation.
Not clinging to these two views is what is called an Arhat.
Clinging greedily to gain and offerings, one is unable to liberate oneself.
Because they are able to eliminate that attachment, they are called Arhats.
"This is the dharma of the householder; this is the dharma of the renunciant"—when ordinary people give rise to such discrimination, one should effect the liberation from that attachment.
Within all phenomena, one perceives inferiority and superiority;
clinging to what is a fit vessel and what is not, one should understand and release such clinging.
Remaining far removed from the dharmas of ordinary beings, one takes the Buddha-dharmas as one's object.
One should preach the Dharma for them, free from attachment to gain or non-gain.
Whether great or small, phenomena are not solid; such things are exceedingly numerous.
One should thereby resolve their attachments, for the characteristics of sentient beings are thus.
They are able to produce all the marks and signs, and their deeds are likewise manifold;
only those who are disciplined and supple can eliminate the conceptualization of such signs.
The wondrous worlds of the Buddhas arise from the cultivation of a pure mind.
One should eliminate the perception of that world.
Nirvana is neither nirvana nor non-nirvana; it can be produced, yet it cannot be produced.
This practice is the path to bodhi; herein one does not seek bodhi.
There are those with evil precepts and those with virtuous precepts; there are those with merit and those without merit.
Foolish and wise sentient beings alike manifest various appearances.
Such sentient beings possess many diverse perceptions.
To eliminate such perceptions, one should preach the Dharma for them:
"This is a fertile field of merit; this is not a fertile field of merit";
distinguishing between the dharmas of the foolish and the wise, these matters are likewise manifold.
Grasping at the notion of "woman," one likewise discriminates "man";
distinguishing between "this is noble" and "this is not noble," one gives rise to dualistic views.
Sentient beings, lacking the heart of wisdom, give rise to these two views.
Those who cling to these two views should have them eliminated.
Whether regressive or non-regressive, determinate or indeterminate;
this is close to enlightenment, while that is not close to enlightenment.
Having already attained awakening, they enter ultimate parinirvāṇa;
practicing with such characteristics, they discriminate nirvāṇa.
Only those who are disciplined and supple eliminate this notion of sentient beings.
This is called an Arhat, and is also called one who has eliminated conceptualization.
This is the dharma of a Bodhisattva, yet it is designated by the name "Arhat";
if one perceives this fundamental cause, one knows him to be an Arhat.
“In this way, Ānanda!
By the power of skillful means, the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, speaks of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas for the sake of śrāvakas as being ‘arhats.’”
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
Why does the Tathāgata call a bodhisattva mahāsattva a 'śrāvaka'?
Ānanda, you should know this!"

Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cause immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings to hear the sound of the Buddha-dharma, the sound of the inconceivable dharma, the sound of the dharma of tranquil enlightenment, the sound of the dharma free from conceptual proliferation, and the sound of the stainless, pure dharma, they are called Śrāvakas.

Furthermore, by means of the sound of Nirvana as the incomparable Dharma and the Dharma of peace and bliss, and by means of the sounds of the applications of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path, they cause many sentient beings to be able to diligently seek them quickly; thus they are called Śrāvakas.
He speaks of this body as empty and not a solid dharma, for solidity cannot be found; yet ordinary, foolish beings are greedily attached to this body—this is the sound of his explanation.

Furthermore, he speaks of what is seen by the eye-faculty as illusory, teaching that one should give rise to the Buddha-eye and the inconceivable Dharma-eye; through these eyes, he causes many sentient beings to be free from delusion—this is the sound of his explanation.
Moreover, he speaks of all dharmas as having the characteristic of non-arising; this is called the sound of the Śrāvaka.

Furthermore, it is said that sounds are like echoes; one should not give rise to defiled attachment toward them. There is no hearer and no speaker. One should not give rise to the perception of smelling regarding fragrances, for there is no one who smells a fragrance. It is like a person in a dream who smells many fragrances; in reality, there is neither fragrance nor one who smells it. Due to inversion, the perception of smelling fragrance arises. These fragrances are like dream-phenomena: they are untrustworthy and lack solidity. To speak of these sounds of the Dharma is called being a Śrāvaka.

Furthermore, it is said that the tongue-faculty (*jihvā-āyatana*) is like a piece of meat that cannot perceive taste; this piece of meat is like a mass of foam, truly having no substantial existence. Likewise, the perception of taste is inconceivable, and the realm of taste (*rasa-dhātu*) is without mind. Being free from all mental factors (*citta-dharma*), one should not give rise to the mind; knowing that the mind is characterized by non-abiding, one causes sentient beings to hear the sound of such teachings—this is called a "Hearer" (*śrāvaka*).

Furthermore, regarding this Dharma, they perceive it clearly and directly; according to what they have seen, they are able to utter sounds to proclaim it. Moreover, they declare that this body is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature or characteristics; because it is without characteristics, it is neither produced nor is there anything produced. For the sake of many sentient beings, they speak these sounds of the Dharma of Bodhi; such are called Śrāvakas.

Furthermore, it is taught that the sphere of mind (manāyatana) is empty, non-existent, and devoid of intrinsic nature; it is like an illusion, neither arising nor ceasing. One who hears this teaching of the Dharma is called a śrāvaka.

Furthermore, it is said that there is an inconceivable gift of Dharma; this Dharma can attain bodhi. Since bodhi is inconceivable, the gift of Dharma is also inconceivable, for it can give rise to the inconceivable qualities of bodhi.
Why is this so? Just as it is with the seed, so it is with the fruit; herein there is no fruit, yet fruit is spoken of by means of sound.

Furthermore, it is said that material giving is inferior while the gift of Dharma is supreme. By removing the mind of stinginess, one is without discrimination and does not give rise to the notion of "giving. Just as a magician makes no discrimination regarding his illusions, so too, by practicing giving with a mind free from discrimination, one can generate bodhi. To speak of these sounds of the Dharma is what is called being a śrāvaka.

This sound is free from all verbal expression and brings to rest all afflictions; it transcends all speech and is detached from all defilement and attachment, yet through this very sound, it proclaims the Buddha-dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because this sound is the most supreme among all sounds. By means of this sound, the Buddha-dharma is proclaimed;

this sound is indestructible and has no basis, arising from that which is non-dual and undifferentiated, and it proclaims the non-dual and undifferentiated Buddha-dharma in accordance with its own arising.
"Therefore, Ānanda!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva causes sentient beings to hear such sounds of the Dharma, they are called śrāvakas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"By means of the inconceivable, supreme sound of the Buddha-dharma,
they cause many sentient beings to hear the name and fame of the Bodhisattvas.
For the sake of many sentient beings, they are able to preach the tranquility of bodhi."
Pure and free from conceptual proliferation—this is called a śrāvaka.
Proclaiming the bliss of nirvāṇa, a bliss beyond compare;
and teaching the characteristic of cessation—this is called a śrāvaka.
They teach the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of awakening;
because they swiftly give rise to these dharmas, they are called śrāvakas.
They proclaim that this body is empty and that its solidity cannot be found.
For the sake of ordinary beings and those of limited scope, he clearly explains the characteristics of this body.
He further teaches that what is perceived within the sense-base of the eye is entirely illusory;
yet ignorant sentient beings give rise to defiled delusions regarding it.
One should give rise to the Buddha-eye, the inconceivable eye of equanimity;
within the dharma of non-arising, one likewise does not produce delusion or attachment.
Knowing that sound is like an echo, one understands that the ear is likewise so.
In this, there is no one who hears, nor is there anyone who speaks.
Because there is neither hearing nor speaking, one should not give rise to defiled attachment.
To proclaim and reveal this to all sentient beings—this is what is called a śrāvaka.
Just as when a person in a dream Smells various kinds of fragrances;
These arise merely based on inversion, Yet in reality, nothing exists.
One should know the nose in this way: It cannot smell those fragrances.
For the sake of sentient beings who are deluded, the Bodhisattva proclaims this:
he says that the tongue is empty and non-existent; it is a piece of flesh that does not know taste.
If the flesh could know taste, it should be able to know it when touched by the hand.
Thus he proclaims this perception: that the perception of flavor has many faults;
one should know that this realm of flavor is inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva, being without dependence, is able to perceive it clearly and directly.
One who proclaims the directly perceived Dharma is called a śrāvaka.
One proclaims that such a body is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature or characteristics;
because it is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature or characteristics, it is neither produced nor has anything been produced.
Bodhi is also like this: it is unarisen and has nothing that arises;
for the sake of many sentient beings it is taught, and thus they are called śrāvakas.
It teaches the nature and characteristics of the sense-bases and elements, yet in reality, these do not exist at all.
Because they teach the Dharma of non-existence, they are called Śrāvakas.
They proclaim the Dharma of giving; this gift of Dharma is inconceivable.
From this giving, the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Buddha is born.
The gift of material wealth is inferior; the gift of Dharma is supreme.
It can eliminate the mind of stinginess and greed, leading one to the fruit of Bodhi.
It is free from all sounds of verbal explanation and brings to rest all sounds of affliction.
A voice free from all defilement and attachment, a stainless and pure voice;
a most supreme and subtle voice, whose very nature is tranquility;
with this tranquil voice, he proclaims the inconceivable Buddha-dharma.
This sound is indestructible and likewise has no basis;
it is said to be non-dual and without distinction, and is therefore called "śrāvaka.
By means of such sounds, they proclaim what all Buddhas have taught.
Speaking in accordance with sounds, one seeks the path to Bodhi;
constantly proclaiming it for others, one purifies the Buddha-worlds—
the supreme path of the World Teachers, the dwelling place of all Buddhas.
This trichiliocosm is said to abide like empty space;
as all sentient beings are like space, they all share the same characteristic as nirvāṇa.
The forty-four [dharmas] that have been taught serve to distinguish among sentient beings.
All are like space—ineffable and without discrimination.
This realm is likewise; do not give rise to the notion of solidity.
Herein there is no birth-and-death, nor are there afflictions to be extinguished.
Among births, no dharma is born, nor is there any sentient being;
because all these are quiescent, there is no one who sees birth.
Constantly I preach for the sake of sentient beings, day and night without ceasing.
Yet they do not give rise to this thought: "I am teaching for the sake of sentient beings.
The śrāvakas understand in this way and likewise teach for the sake of sentient beings;
because they are able to hear what has not been heard, they are called śrāvakas.
With a courageous mind, he proclaims the supreme Dharma;
if one can understand this Dharma, one also understands the suchness of all phenomena.
Thus do the Śrāvakas speak: it is undefiled and without outflows.
For the sake of many sentient beings, he also preaches the Dharma free from defilement and attachment.
If one knows the realm of non-defilement, which is pure and free from conceptual proliferation,
then even if one desires to contemplate it among all the Buddha-dharmas, one cannot see it.
The Dharma taught by all Buddhas is not seen from afar;
nor is it present nearby, yet those who can perceive it exist.
When the Śrāvakas preach this Dharma, they cause many sentient beings to have faith.
Abiding securely within this Dharma, one is therefore called a śrāvaka.
By virtue of these matters, Ānanda, I speak of them as śrāvakas;
you should know that such śrāvakas are bodhisattvas who rely on nothing.
"Therefore, Ānanda!
By the power of skillful means, the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, speaks of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas as being 'śrāvakas' for the sake of those who are śrāvakas."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
Why does the Tathāgata refer to a bodhisattva mahāsattva by the name 'pratyekabuddha'?
Ānanda, you should know this!"

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva clearly perceives all phenomena through direct vision; because of this clear perception through direct vision, they are able to know the noble dharmas, yet they neither increase nor decrease any phenomena, awakening to the fact that all phenomena are without increase or decrease. One who possesses such clear perception through direct vision is called a Pratyekabuddha.

He awakens to and knows all inconceivable dharmas; he awakens to and knows that all sentient beings are identical to nirvāṇa, which is unobtainable, neither arising nor ceasing. Because it neither arises nor ceases, it is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). He illuminates the limit of nirvāṇa, the limit of sentient beings, the limit of the non-existence of all dharmas, the limit of names, and the limit of the ineffable. It does not rely on verbal expression, nor can it be expressed by words.

Why is this? Because when one speaks of the emptiness of dharmas, one does not attain mastery; when one speaks, one cannot know the limit of sentient beings (*sattvānta*) nor the limit of dharmas (*dharmānta*). To clearly perceive and fully awaken to these limits is called a *pratyekabuddha*.

When one perceives the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) through verbal designation, it is called the "aggregate of form"; yet this aggregate of form possesses no verbal designation. Because it is free from verbal designation, it is merely by means of verbal designation that it is named the "aggregate of form," and herein there is neither self nor what belongs to a self.
Why is this so? Both speech and the speaker are empty;

they lack self-mastery and are neither born nor extinguished. Since speech is devoid of cognition, how could it declare, "This is the aggregate of form," or "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness"?

One should likewise clearly perceive this: the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is designated as the "aggregate of consciousness" only by means of verbal expression; yet this aggregate of consciousness is devoid of verbal expression, for it is beyond all expression. It is merely through verbal expression that it is called the "aggregate of consciousness," and herein there is no self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).
Why is this so? Both speech and the speaker are empty; they lack autonomy and are neither born nor extinguished.
Speech is devoid of cognition; how then could it declare, "This is the aggregate of consciousness"?
One who clearly perceives the various conditions for the verbal designations of these five aggregates is called a Pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? Because regarding these verbal designations of the aggregates and their various conditions, he is able to know that these conditions are neither with conditions nor without conditions.
"Ānanda! This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is called a pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Directly perceiving all phenomena, one knows that the noble Dharma is likewise;
it is free from contention, indestructible, and ultimately devoid of marks.
Directly perceiving all phenomena, their intrinsic nature and characteristics are themselves empty.
If one knows the characteristic of intrinsic nature To be ultimately non-existent,
And has already attained this direct vision, Being no different from that Dharma;
This is called perfect awakening, The inconceivable Pratyekabuddha.
Sentient beings are like nirvāṇa; their beginning cannot be found.
Without beginning or end, this is called the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Sentient beings are like nirvāṇa; ultimately, there is no birth.
If phenomena have no arising, they are called nirvāṇa.
Sentient beings are like nirvāṇa, for they also possess various functions of illumination;
since these functions of illumination lack a self, they are called nirvāṇa.
Sentient beings are like nirvāṇa; various names are established for them.
They neither arise nor cease; they are spoken of only by means of verbal expression.
The nature of verbal expression is empty, and in verbal expression there is nothing known.
Because there is nothing to be known, sentient beings are nirvāṇa.
Discourse lacks autonomy; there is no self and no mind.
Since discourse has no intrinsic nature, it ultimately possesses nothing at all.
Speech does not rely on limits, nor does it abide anywhere;
that which is spoken by speech is the inconceivable limit of sentient beings.
The limit of sentient beings is nirvāṇa; it is the inconceivable reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Peaceful and free from conceptual proliferation, it is the supreme place of refuge.
Like the limit of a flash of lightning, it is the very limit of sentient beings;
without conditions and without location, it is the inconceivable reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The limit of all phenomena has no manifold names;
because it is designated by names, that limit cannot be apprehended.
The ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) cannot be named, nor is there anyone who can know it.
The limit of sentient beings is selfless; one should know that this limit is empty.
Speech does not rely on a limit, for speech has nothing to proclaim.
If one can understand this, there is no such thing as the limit of sentient beings.
To speak of "emptiness of non-mastery" is to speak of not knowing the various limits;
that which is spoken and that which is expressed is the inconceivable limit of sentient beings.
Such limits as these can be naturally and spontaneously awakened to and known.
This is called Perfect Enlightenment, the inconceivable Pratyekabuddha.
One perceives the aggregate of form through names and thus speaks of it;
yet this aggregate is beyond speech, for it is eternally free from verbal expression.
Distant from that which is known— wherein "that which is known" is designated as "life"—
one who can know this object of knowledge has no place of abiding.
Regarding the aggregates of name-and-form that have been taught, within the aggregate of form there is no self.
Speech is empty of self-mastery; ultimately, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
The nature of that which is spoken is ultimately non-existent;
because it is non-existent, one is able to speak the name of the aggregate of form.
Feeling and perception are likewise, and volitional formations and consciousness are also thus;
because they are beyond verbal expression, these are called the "five aggregates.
These aggregates cannot be described, nor can they be severed.
Neither arising nor ceasing, there is no place that is not impermanent.
It is not the escape from afflictions, nor is it retribution or karma;
it is neither grasping nor abandoning, and it is not the cessation of conceptual proliferation.
It is neither śamatha nor vipaśyanā;
it is neither excessive desire nor contentment, neither indolence nor diligence.
It is neither restlessness nor regret, and it is without increase or decrease.
One cannot grasp the dharmas that arise and thereby establish them as precepts.
Without cultivating non-discrimination, one proclaims non-discrimination;
without fear and without contention, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
By means of these words of discourse, there is nothing for discourse to enter;
discourse and all phenomena are spoken without discourse.
Being able to personally attain direct realization, one preaches the Dharma without end.
Relying upon such samādhi, one does not cling to any verbal expressions.
Possessing this directly perceived wisdom, one knows the equality of all speech;
thus, while all phenomena are expressed through words, they are spoken by means of wordlessness.
Having already attained this direct realization, he no longer follows others;
he is called a Perfectly Awakened One, an inconceivable Pratyekabuddha.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva directly perceives that ignorance and volitional formations do not give rise to conceptualization, and knows the intrinsic nature of consciousness, the intrinsic nature of name-and-form, the intrinsic nature of the six sense bases, the intrinsic nature of contact, the intrinsic nature of feeling, the intrinsic nature of craving, the intrinsic nature of grasping, the intrinsic nature of becoming, the intrinsic nature of birth, and the intrinsic nature of aging and death—clearly and directly knowing these phenomena within this Dharma—he is called a pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Directly observing ignorance, one sees that it ultimately cannot arise;
Like a reflection in water, it has no existence from beginning to end."
Clearly seeing all phenomena, yet without any sign of movement;
if one sees phenomena in this way, for that reason it is called "clarity.
The nature of clarity is like space, and all phenomena are likewise so.
If one attains this direct vision, he is called a Pratyekabuddha.
As it is said: "The activities of this body do not exist within, nor do they exist without; these bodily activities are unarisen."
The activities of the body are like a plantain tree; ultimately, they possess no solidity.
Neither arising nor ceasing, their nature is like space.
When fearless bodhisattvas attain this direct realization, [they see it thus].
This is called perfect awakening; such are the inconceivable pratyekabuddhas.
They thoroughly understand that all phenomena are by nature eternally like illusions;
they are also able to have deep faith and understanding that consciousness has no inherent existence.
Observing such consciousness, its activity is seen to be illusory;
because of this knowledge, one is able to know that the nature of consciousness is empty.
Having known that wisdom is not a knowing subject, one remains unstained in all circumstances.
If one knows such dharmas, consciousness is then identical to an illusion.
As it is said regarding all name-and-form (nāmarūpa), they are without sensation and cannot be described;
yet knowing their nature and characteristics, they are ultimately non-existent.
One can explain the nature of the sense bases (āyatana) Without grasping at their characteristics;
To know the bases in this way Is because their nature is emptiness (śūnyatā).
The nature of contact is omnipresent, Abiding within all the sense bases.
When observing this contact, it is like an illusion and non-existent.
The nature of contact is originally empty; it is through conceptualization that one can know it.
Yet as for the nature of these various contacts, they have no fixed location or place where they abide.
If one can directly perceive contact, the wise are able to remain far removed from it;
possessing wisdom and remaining detached from contact, such a person is called a Pratyekabuddha.
One who can know that the characteristics of sensation are empty, and that sensation likewise lacks intrinsic nature—
Like a bubble, it is not solid; ultimately, it is nothing at all.
Having severed all craving and attained mastery over the dharma of non-craving, having reached the state where craving is exhausted—one is called a Pratyekabuddha.
Knowing that grasping has nothing to grasp, one also knows it to be empty and non-existent;
it does not arise as anything substantial, like water in a mirage during the heat of the day.
All original perceptions of existence, as well as original perceptions of birth;
If one knows that this nature of perception is ultimately non-existent,
having already transcended all aging and no longer undergoing death,
one shall no longer receive a body in any place whatsoever.
Having attained this direct vision, there is nothing upon which to rely;
by means of the name "Pratyekabuddha," he proclaims the various Bodhisattvas.
"Thus it is, Ānanda!"
The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by the power of skillful means, speaks of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva for the sake of śrāvakas, calling him a pratyekabuddha.
It is thus, Ānanda!

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as being called those of firm faith, those of firm dharma, those on the eighth stage, srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda spoke these verses:
"The Sovereign Guide and Teacher, Speaks that which is ineffable;
He ties knots within the void, And unties them while they are still empty."
The Buddha possesses great skillful means, preaching the Dharma of non-attachment;
regarding that which is inexpressible, he is able to explain it through differentiation.
*The Sutra of the Vast, Pure, and Unregressing Wheel*, Fascicle Three.
The Sutra on the Vast, Extensive, Pure, and Unregressing Wheel Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Four.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhìyán of Liangzhou during the Song Dynasty.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

All the world will surely give rise to doubt and be unable to understand why the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, speaks of those with firm faith, those who follow the Dharma by firm adherence, and so forth, up to the Pratyekabuddhas.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
“Ānanda, you should know!
If there are sentient beings who have performed various wholesome deeds under previous Buddhas, they will be able to understand the Tathāgata’s esoteric speech and give rise to no doubt.”
Why is this? Because they are able to understand the Tathāgata’s esoteric language as being like an illusion, like a mirage in the heat, like what is seen in a dream, like a shadow, and like an echo.
Ānanda! One who understands the secret language in this way will not give rise to doubt or confusion.
Therefore, Ānanda!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand the secret language of the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in this way:
if there are those who exert themselves with diligence yet do not attain diligence, or who diligently cultivate wisdom yet do not attain wisdom, they should give rise to no doubt or perplexity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The Buddhas, guides of the world, Speak subtle and secret words difficult to understand;
To inspire great adornment, They teach no differently than the Bodhisattvas.”
Those who are indolent and lacking wisdom cannot decipher the secret language;
therefore, one should apply oneself with diligent vigor for the sake of deciphering that secret language.
Like a magical illusion, a mirage, or a dream, and like a flash of lightning or an echo;
Through verbal expression, these and all such dharmas are manifested.
Thus one knows the subtle and secret words spoken by the Buddhas;
with such wisdom, one can illuminate the pure, subtle, and secret knowledge.
One should not know enlightenment in such a way as to be able to proclaim it;
one should realize it thus: because it is beyond verbal expression, it is empty.
Emptiness cannot know emptiness, nor does emptiness discriminate emptiness.
Severing all conceptual discrimination, one reveals such emptiness.
Like space, there is nowhere to return; there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
Because there is no grasping or abandoning, one thereby knows that phenomena are empty.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If one knows that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are entirely like a dream and remains free from negligence, one will not give rise to doubt or confusion."

When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred million bhikṣus who had conceived the thought of firm faith rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, bared their right shoulders, placed their right knees on the ground, and with single-minded palms joined together in unison, stood before the Buddha and spoke these verses:
“Today the Honored Muni has removed our doubts;
Having attained understanding of the subtle and secret meaning, We seek bodhi through faith.”

Furthermore, there were five hundred million bhikṣus who had conceived the thought of the firm Dharma; having heard these verses from the bhikṣus, they immediately rose from their seats, and so forth, joining their palms and standing before the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
“Now, having received the illumination of Bodhi, We have removed the darkness of our doubts;
Having attained the understanding of the subtle and secret meaning, We seek Bodhi through the firm Dharma.”

Furthermore, there were ten billion bhikṣus who harbored the notion of being "eighth-rank" practitioners (*aṣṭamaka*). Having heard these verses from the bhikṣus, they immediately rose from their seats and, proceeding until they had assembled together, stood before the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"The minds that previously dwelt on the stage of the eighth rank— Today we have all abandoned them;
Having attained the understanding of the subtle and secret meaning, The eighth-rank practitioners seek awakening."

Furthermore, there were one billion one hundred million bhikṣus who had conceived the notion that they had attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. Having heard these verses from the other bhikṣus, they immediately rose from their seats, gathered together, stood before the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"Now, within the Buddha’s Dharma, We have severed the net of all doubts;
Having understood the Buddha’s subtle and secret words, We proclaim the attainment of *srotāpanna*."

Furthermore, there were twenty-five thousand bhikṣus who had conceived the notion of being *sakṛdāgāmins*. Having heard these verses from the bhikṣus, they immediately rose from their seats, and having gathered together, stood before the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"We were formerly deeply attached, Our minds delighting in the state of a *sakṛdāgāmin*;
Now we have all attained freedom from attachment, Tranquil extinction, free from conceptual proliferation."

Furthermore, there were five billion bhikṣus who had conceived the notion that they had attained the stage of *anāgāmin*. Upon hearing these verses from the bhikṣus, they immediately rose from their seats, gathered together, stood before the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"Now we have encountered the World-Honored Savior, Who has distanced himself from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
Having obtained the illumination of the light of Bodhi, He has forever uprooted all notions of fruition."

Furthermore, there were thirty-five trillion bhikṣus who had attained the fourth dhyāna and harbored the notion that they were arhats. Upon hearing these verses from the other bhikṣus, they immediately rose from their seats, gathered together, and stood before the Buddha, speaking these verses:
“I have already left afflictions behind, And have realized the non-dual Dharma;
I know the equality of all vehicles, For they are all like illusory phenomena.”

Furthermore, there were twenty thousand bhikṣus who had conceived the notion of being śrāvakas; having heard the verses spoken by those bhikṣus, they immediately rose from their seats and, proceeding until they were assembled together, stood before the Buddha and spoke these verses:
“The Muni, the Honored One, free from all bonds, Has ceased our empty prattle;
You have secretly taught the meaning for śrāvakas, Which we have now fully mastered.”

Furthermore, there were five thousand bhikṣus who had conceived the thought of being pratyekabuddhas; having heard these verses from the other bhikṣus, they immediately rose from their seats and, proceeding until they were gathered together, stood before the Buddha and spoke these verses:
“We now clearly behold The conduct of the pratyekabuddhas;
We understand the subtle and secret meaning of the Buddha— The inconceivable pratyekabuddhas.”

Furthermore, there were ten thousand bhikṣuṇīs who had conceived the notion of the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the notion of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the notion of the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and the notion of the fruit of *arhat*. Having heard the verses spoken by the bhikṣus, they immediately rose from their seats, gathered together, stood before the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"Now we know the Dharma of equality, The female state is forever severed;
The Buddha’s words are never otherwise— We shall surely become the Honored One among Men."

Furthermore, there were eighty-eight thousand *upāsakas* who conceived the notion of the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, and the fruit of *anāgāmin*. Having heard these verses from the bhikṣus, they immediately rose from their seats and, having gathered together, stood before the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"Our minds are free from defilement, Like pure *vaiḍūrya* crystal;
For the sake of cultivating the Buddha-dharma, We shall go forth into homelessness this very day."
At that time, sixty billion nayutas of devas in the sky scattered celestial māndārava flowers over the Buddha. Having scattered them, they stood there and spoke these verses:
"Formerly there were conceptions of various vehicles, And there were also conceptions of various fruits;
Today these are all abandoned and relinquished— You will surely attain bodhi."

At that time, there were hundreds of thousands of arhats—Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Aniruddha, Revata, Kapphiṇa, and others—who rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with single-minded palms joined together, all in unison stood before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

Today our aspirations are fulfilled; we have been able to subdue Māra and crush all enemies. We have fully accomplished the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*). Today we have fully attained the merits of the five sensual desires. Today we are fully possessed of false views and have abandoned right view. Today we have taken the lives of many hundreds of thousands of sentient beings. Today we have already reached Bodhi; this very day, we enter parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and said nothing.
Thereupon, hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in the assembly were all filled with doubt and confusion, thinking:
"We are now as if in darkness; how can these great arhats speak in such a manner?"
"How much more so for ordinary people, who, due to doubt, cannot go from here to there, nor from there to here; they cannot stand when seated, nor sit when standing.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, knowing the doubts in the minds of these hundreds of thousands of beings, and by the power of the Buddha, asked the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī:

"Now this great assembly of hundreds of thousands of beings, having heard the words spoken by these venerable bhikṣus, has all given rise to doubt. The World-Honored One remains silent and says nothing. I pray that Mañjuśrī will explain the cause and conditions: for what reason have these venerable bhikṣus spoken such cryptic words?"
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
“Ānanda, you should know!

This is the matter of the stage of non-retrogression for bodhisattvas; only a bodhisattva who has reached non-retrogression is able to realize and understand these secret words of the great virtuous bhikṣus.”
The Venerable Ānanda asked Mañjuśrī,
“Are all these venerable bhikṣus bodhisattvas who have attained the stage of non-retrogression?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"So it is, so it is! These venerable bhikṣus are all bodhisattvas who have attained non-retrogression from awakening.
Ānanda then addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“May you, O virtuous bhikṣus, explain the meaning of these subtle and secret words. Mañjuśrī replied:
“Ignorance (*avidyā*) can give rise to birth and death; therefore it is called ‘mother. Because one cuts off ignorance, it is called ‘killing the mother.’”
The father consists of improper reflection and craving; because one has eternally severed these, it is called "killing the father.
Because all dharmas are indestructible, yet by means of skillful means one destroys manifold perceptions and also destroys all conditioned formations, it is called "destroying the Saṃgha."

One who should destroy the dharmas of ordinary beings is called an arhat; because one does not employ the means of cessation yet destroys the notion of being an arhat, this is called "killing an arhat. Because one does not employ the means of cessation yet destroys the notion of a Tathāgata, this is called "shedding the blood of a Buddha. Such notions as these have already been severed and destroyed, leaving nothing whatsoever remaining.
"Ānanda!
For this reason, the venerable bhikṣus spoke these words:
'Today we have fully accomplished the five deeds of immediate retribution.'"

Why is this so? Because within this Dharma there is no accumulation, no dispersal, no decrease, and no increase; therefore, it is called the fulfillment and accomplishment of the five deeds of immediate retribution.
Ānanda, you should know!

As for those who say, "Today we have fully accomplished the merits of the five desires," those bhikṣus understand these five desires to be like a dream, like an illusion, like a mirage in the heat, like a shadow, and like an echo. Having fully accomplished this wisdom, they experience neither increase nor decrease regarding the five desires.
Why is this? Because one is able to know that these phenomena are ultimately non-existent.

Since they are non-existent, one can know them as they truly are; thus, by attaining such patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) regarding those phenomena, one is said to be fully accomplished in the merit of the five sensual desires.
"Ānanda! For this reason, those bhikṣus speak thus:
'Today we have fully accomplished and perfected the merits of the five desires.'"
"Ānanda, you should know that when they say,
'Today we have fully accomplished wrong views and abandoned right views,' those bhikṣus recognize all phenomena as wrong and perceive all phenomena as wrong."

Ānanda! That which is called "false" refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), which are entirely illusory. These illusory phenomena are like empty space—neither increasing nor decreasing, neither abiding in any direction nor belonging to anything.
Why is this? Because they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
He knows that all these phenomena are entirely equal; because they are equal, right view is also equal, and he has already distanced himself from such conceptualizations of equality.
Why is this? Because while there may be perceptions of equality and perceptions of inequality, those bhikṣus possess neither perception of equality nor perception of inequality. Why is this?
The Dharma of all Buddhas is free from all conceptualizations; they have realized the non-arising of the Buddha-Dharma, yet they do not apprehend that dharma of non-arising.
Therefore, Ānanda, those great virtuous bhikṣus speak these words:
"Today we have fully accomplished wrong views and abandoned right view.
Ānanda, you should know that they speak thus:
"Regarding the statement, 'Today we have slain the lives of many hundreds of thousands of beings,' Ānanda!

Those bhikṣus cause the hundreds of thousands of beings—gods and humans—present in this assembly to know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are entirely like an illusion, like a shadow, and like an echo. Because they know these dharmas, they abandon the notion of a being (*sattvasaṃjñā*), the notion of a life-span (*jīvasaṃjñā*), and the notion of a person (*pudgalasaṃjñā*); they abandon the notion of all dharmas, and through various skillful means, they plant the roots of merit for bodhi within all dharmas."

The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, having heard these secret words from the bhikṣus, shall likewise be freed from the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, and the notion of a person, and shall not die again and again.

Why is this? If one clings to the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, or the notion of a person, one dies again and again; because such a person has already distanced themselves from these dharmas, they will ultimately not be born.
Therefore, Ānanda!
Those bhikṣus will speak thus:
"Today we have destroyed the life-faculties of many hundreds of thousands of living beings."
