"Ānanda, you should know that those who say,
'Today we have attained awakening and entered parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder,' Ānanda!"

Those bhikṣus shall cause this great assembly—consisting of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of devas and humans—to attain liberation from afflictions and reach bodhi this very day.

Why is this? Because this great assembly has all resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and having today heard the teaching on the adamantine words (*vajrapada*), they have all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and have beheld bodhi. For this reason, it is said:

"Today we have attained bodhi; today we enter parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder. This means that they do not sever afflictions nor cultivate the Buddha-dharmas, yet they possess no remaining afflictions.
Therefore, Ānanda!
Those bhikṣus will speak thus:
"Today we have attained awakening and entered parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder."
"Regarding what is called 'this day,' Ānanda, you should know that on this very day there is neither arising nor anything that arises; therefore it is named 'this day.
In the correct phonetics of India, the sound for 'non-arising' (ajāta) is identical to the sound for 'this day' (adya). For this reason, Ānanda!"

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family seeking the Bodhisattva vehicle should resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should gradually diminish their attachment to all phenomena. By resolving upon bodhicitta through the principle of non-apprehensibility (*anupalabdha*), one is said to have the thought of renunciation regarding all phenomena; regarding all phenomena, this is called entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and attaining parinirvāṇa.

Ānanda! A son of noble family who seeks the Bodhisattva vehicle should not be deeply attached to the perception of the sun, nor should he give rise to the perception of day because of the sun. Ānanda!
Foolish and inferior people conceive of the day as being permanent because they lack wisdom. Why is this?
If this day were real, firm, and eternal, it would have to be accumulated and could not pass away; there would only be day and no night.
Ānanda, you should know!
Those who possess the perception of day and night are ordinary and inferior beings.
Therefore, Ānanda!
Noble sons who seek the Bodhisattva vehicle and possess a profound resolve are protected by spiritual friends; they should not give rise to the perception of day or night. Why is this?
"Seeking liberation from all conceptualizations is the path to Bodhi.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Ignorance is called the mother, For it is able to give birth to birth-and-death;
Having uprooted its very foundation, it is therefore called "harm.
Improper contemplation and reflection—craving and delight—are called its "father.
One knows them all as they truly are: ultimately, they do not exist at all.
Because one knows there is nothing, one harms its very root;
because one does not rely on "nothingness," this is therefore called "harming.
This refers to the dharmas of the Arhat and the dharmas of the ordinary person.
He has already destroyed them by means of wisdom; therefore, it is called "harming.
Having known the nature and characteristics of all the manifold marks, he destroys those marks by means of the indestructible Dharma—this is called "destroying the Saṃgha."
Originally, that which was discriminated as the Tathāgata’s various conceptions of dharmas has already been severed and distanced; one knows them to be neither arising nor ceasing.
These conceptions arise in succession, and through deliberation, one knows them to be empty.
As for the equality thus described, he has already been able to realize it.
Regarding the qualities of desire that were mentioned, their names are of five kinds;
having distanced himself from all such perceptions, he knows that all perceptions are like illusions.
These bhikṣus, with neither increase nor decrease regarding desire,
spoke thus before the Teacher who guides the world:
"We know that the nature of desire is entirely empty, just like what is seen in a dream."
Ultimately there is nothing that arises; herein one attains fulfillment in wisdom.
Knowing phenomena through false wisdom, one sees them as deceptive and unstable;
"false" means illusory and unreal; herein one attains fulfillment in wisdom.
Conditioned phenomena are illusory, yet they possess neither distance nor proximity;
being without cognition, they have no nearness or farness, like five fingers rubbing against space.
Those who speak of right views all perceive this as equality.
As all phenomena are equal, so too are knowledge and vision.
The ordinary and the small possess much conceptual discrimination; because of the notion of a "sentient being," they die.
If one does not perceive a sentient being, then there is also no notion of death.
For all sentient beings who possess conditions, remove their notion of a life-span;
knowing the faults of conceiving a life-span, remove such a notion.
Be far removed from the notion of a sentient being as well as the notion of a life-span.
He speaks thus: "Having harmed the lives of many beings, he has already distanced himself from the perception of death;
having realized the non-conceptual Dharma, he knows that enlightenment is indestructible, neither increasing nor subject to fruitless retribution."
Birth and death cannot be gathered together; one awakens to the pure dharma.
All dharmas are without contention; they do not arise and are eternally quiescent.
One should not differentiate day, nor should one differentiate night.
Within the dharma that neither comes nor goes, one seeks awakening.
Ordinary beings and the small-vehicle practitioners constantly engage in discrimination, taking the passing of daily activities for the day itself;
those who seek awakening should not make such discriminations.
"By means of these secret words, he has proclaimed such a Dharma;
because he understands this Dharma, he is able to speak in this way.

When the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī had spoken these verses, at that time hundreds of thousands of sentient beings within the assembly had their arrows of doubt extracted. Free from further uncertainty, they attained great illumination and realized the patience of the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Each of them removed the upper robe they were wearing and offered it to the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying these words:
“May we, in future ages, preach this sublime Dharma and awaken sentient beings, just as the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī awakens sentient beings now.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
"To dispel the doubts of sentient beings and illuminate the Buddha-dharma, the Dharma ought to be thus.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Are not all these hundreds of thousands of sentient beings now having the arrows of doubt extracted and severed by the World-Honored One?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"These hundreds of thousands of sentient beings were all originally taught and brought to maturity in awakening by Mañjuśrī; upon hearing his preaching of the Dharma, they were all able to believe and understand it."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Are all these sentient beings non-retrogressive regarding bodhi?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"So it is, so it is! These sentient beings have already become non-retrogressive regarding bodhi. Why is this?
“Because they are protected and sustained by the spiritual friend Mañjuśrī.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

"Are all these bhikṣus—who conceive the notion of firm faith, the notion of firm dharma, the notion of the person of the eightfold path, the notion of a srotāpanna, the notion of a sakṛdāgāmin, the notion of an anāgāmin, the notion of an arhat, the notion of a śrāvaka, and the notion of a pratyekabuddha—irreversible from bodhi?"

The Buddha told Ānanda: "This teaching is difficult to believe. Those who delight in inferior dharmas, who are indolent, lazy, and lack diligent perseverance; who are greedily attached to food and drink and greedily attached to sensual desires; who associate with those who take pleasure in practicing the dharma of sensual desire; who enjoy talking about useless matters; whose minds are distracted and who have lost mindfulness, lacking in dignified deportment; whose hearts are restless and turbulent, failing to restrain their sense faculties; who are flighty, playful, foolish, perverse, and talkative—for such beings, it is difficult to believe in this Dharma."

Ānanda! Clinging to overweening pride, they fail to protect their bodies; being greedily attached to life and body, they distance themselves from secluded dwellings and abandon the Dharma of much learning. They break the precepts, are arrogant, and they revile, steal, and do not respect the Dharma. They destroy the True Dharma and are impoverished of the wealth of the Dharma; they delight in what is contrary to the Dharma, slander the True Dharma, and take pleasure in practicing what is contrary to the Dharma. They do not know how to repay kindness, nor do they revere the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Ānanda! It is difficult for such sentient beings to have faith in this Dharma.

With minds of stinginess firmly attached to evil precepts and anger, they do not understand the Buddha-dharma; they possess corrupt wisdom and are impoverished in insight. Protected by evil friends and estranged from virtuous friends, they are not protected by the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor are they protected by the various *dhāraṇī* kings of sutras. They give rise to views of attainment, deeply coveting gain and offerings, and becoming excessively attached to robes and alms bowls. They hold robes and bowl-objects in extreme regard, yet they do not respect their *upādhyāyas* and *ācāryas*, nor do they diligently apply themselves to spiritual practice during the first and last watches of the night.
Ānanda! It is difficult for such sentient beings to have faith in this Dharma.

They commit killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, double-tongued speech, harsh words, and idle chatter; they harbor greed, hatred, and wrong views; they associate with those who hold wrong views; they practice and propagate false and expedient methods; they lack shame and remorse, forming cliques and socializing; they wander alone without companions, departing from the way of the śramaṇa and practicing what is not the way of a śramaṇa; and they do not believe that all phenomena are empty, signless, wishless, unconditioned, unborn, undying, and devoid of the characteristic of destruction.
"Ānanda, you should know that it is difficult for such sentient beings to have faith in this Dharma.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, he remained silent.
At that time, Ānanda, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, asked the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī,
for what reason does the World-Honored One remain silent and say nothing?"

Mañjuśrī said: “In the degenerate age to come, sentient beings will have accomplished such evil and unwholesome dharmas that they will be unable to believe or understand such a profound dharma; for this reason, the World-Honored One remained silent.”
The Venerable Ānanda asked Mañjuśrī,
"Will there be few sentient beings in future ages who have faith and understanding in such a Dharma?
Mañjuśrī replied:

"In future generations, those sentient beings who will have faith in this Dharma will be very few, just as among sentient beings there are many who do not recognize precious jewels and very few who do. Why is this so?
"It is not within the reach of their intellectual power. Ānanda!
It is the same for sentient beings: those who, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, believe and understand it are few."

Should there be those who believe in and understand such a Dharma as this, they will not be honored by the people of their country, cities, or villages; rather, the people of the land will all collectively despise them and keep their distance.
"Why is this? It is because this person, due to the karmic causes and conditions of obstructive deeds committed in previous lives, now undergoes this retribution.
Ānanda then addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"I only pray that you will expound this meaning for the sake of these beings of little faith and understanding.
Mañjuśrī said, "This matter should be asked of the Buddha; the Buddha shall expound it."
At that time, Ānanda immediately questioned the Buddha.

Thereupon the World-Honored One looked around in the four directions and extended his tongue, covering the entire trichiliocosm. From that tongue-mark he further emitted light, which shone throughout the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, pervading them all.

At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, the fourfold assembly all beheld the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, all of whom were preaching this Dharma. Having heard and understood this Dharma, they all gathered together in harmony and entreated the World-Honored One:
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will proclaim this Dharma so that it shall not be severed."
World-Honored One!

Now, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, proclaim this Dharma; we have all been able to see and hear it. The Dharma they preach neither increases nor decreases, being exactly equal and no different from that of the present World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his tongue-phenomenon and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Have you ever seen anyone who speaks untruthful words possess such a broad and long tongue-phenomenon?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“There is none,
World-Honored One.”

This is the tongue-mark obtained as the fruit of omniscience, which the World-Honored One has truthfully proclaimed through his precepts, concentration, patience, compassion, benefit, kindness, pity, joy, and equanimity.
Therefore, World-Honored One!

We only pray that you will expound upon this meaning for the sake of those men and women of good family who possess little faith; by means of this matter, may those who do not yet believe come to understand through these proofs and all attain faith.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"Now, these fourfold assemblies who have gathered here—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others—whoever hears this Dharma taught shall all become non-retrogressive from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. By practicing gradually, they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. In this very place, I proclaim this Dharma without increase or decrease, exactly as it is today, no different at all."

At that time, the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, were all filled with immeasurable joy and leaped for joy.

Among them, some scattered robes over the Buddha, some scattered flowers, and some scattered various garlands, namely: garlands of sumanā, golden garlands, silver garlands, beryl garlands, crystal garlands, musāragalva garlands, agate garlands, emerald garlands, sun-light jewel garlands, and garlands made of the seven kinds of precious jewels. With such garlands as these, they scattered them upon the Buddha.

The devas scattered upon the Buddha various flowers, such as māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, pāruṣaka flowers, mahāpāruṣaka flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, karkārava flowers, mahākarkārava flowers, rocamānī flowers, mahārocamānī flowers, and śukamānī flowers, along with mahāśukamānī flowers. Thus, they scattered these and other such flowers over the Buddha.
Furthermore, they scattered celestial *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers over the Buddha.
In the midst of the sky, they performed celestial music and offered various songs of praise to extol the Buddha’s virtues.
The various dragon kings all rained down pearls, scattering them over the Buddha.

All the women immediately removed the exquisite necklaces from their bodies and scattered them over the Buddha; they took off their garments to offer them to the Buddha, then adjusted their robes, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and stood before the Buddha with palms joined in single-minded devotion. They all spoke these words in unison:
"The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, speak without duality and possess unobstructed wisdom; you have prophesied that we shall certainly become Buddhas."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: “It is so, Ānanda!
These women shall certainly never regress from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

Why is this so? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have forever severed ignorance, greed, hatred, and all forms of pride, defilement, darkness, and every attachment; they have incinerated the afflictions until none remain, and have perfected diligence and the various powers. They possess majestic and dignified authority, mastery of the supernormal bases, and radiance that shines forth; they have perfected their retinue and noble majesty, and are fully endowed with physical beauty, lineage, and status. Possessing the marks and signs of excellence and complete radiance, they have reached the state of peace and security—like Śakra, like Brahmā, and like the lords of the desire realm; they are perfected in deportment, perfected in the practice of precepts, and perfected in discernment.

Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others—all together respect, revere, and praise him who is unstained by worldly dharmas, who has forever abandoned all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma), and who has accomplished the dharma of liberation of all Buddhas; for those who see or hear him, it shall not be in vain.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that what the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have heard is not in vain?”
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Do you not know?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Truly, this has not been known by me; I only pray that you will explain it: how is it that what the Tathāgata hears is never in vain?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen with a single mind; I shall now explain.

Ānanda, you should know that if there are sentient beings who have heard, are hearing, or will hear the name of Śākyamuni Buddha, all such sentient beings shall never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Why is this? Because the Bodhi of all Buddhas is free from falsehood, and is likewise devoid of both greed and hatred. Ānanda!
How much more so for those who today appear before me and are able to scatter even a single flower upon me;

if there are sentient beings who, after my parinirvāṇa, are able to offer even a single flower to my images or relics, such sentient beings shall likewise never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"If there are animals who hear the name of Śākyamuni Buddha, will they all become non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there are any animals who hear the name of Śākyamuni Buddha, all such sentient beings will plant the seeds and conditions for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Why is this so? For all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, those who hear them shall never hear in vain; therefore, the words of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are without duality.
Ānanda! It is like the nyagrodha tree, whose branches and leaves are so luxuriant that they can provide shade for as many as one hundred to five hundred people. Ānanda!
"What do you think?
Is the seed of that tree large or small?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That son is very young.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Although this seed of the nyagrodha tree is small, because it encounters the various conditions of earth, water, fire, wind, and space, it is able to grow and gradually become vast."
Thus it is, Ānanda!
Those sentient beings who plant the seeds of bodhi will gradually cause them to grow until they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; these seeds cannot be rotted and cannot be destroyed.
"Why is this? Because it does not dwell upon any phenomena as a seed, it neither decays nor is it destroyed.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is this due to the power of the original vows of these Buddhas?
Or is it because such is the natural law of the Buddhas?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“This is my original vow: if there are those who hear my name, they shall certainly not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is also the natural law (*dharmatā*) that applies to all Buddhas.”
"Why is this? Because all the dharmas of the Buddhas are equal.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“If all Buddha-dharmas are equal, for what reason do they establish vows?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“When the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, proclaim the Dharma, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the assembly, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, immediately establish vows.”
"May it be so that when I attain Buddhahood in the future and preach the Dharma, seeing or hearing me shall likewise not be in vain.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!"
"Having accomplished such a rare dharma, he further benefits sentient beings through this very dharma.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "So it is, so it is!"
It is as you have said.

For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I have traveled through all buddha-fields to make offerings to the Buddhas, not sparing even my own body or life; I have relinquished all things without stinginess, diligently cultivated and accumulated what is difficult to attain, and, without relying on anything, I have gathered sentient beings by taking no grasp upon any phenomena.
The Sūtra of Vast, Majestic, and Pure [Vows], Scroll Four;
The Sūtra of the Wheel of Non-Retrogression Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Five.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhìyán of Liangzhou during the Song Dynasty.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"It is most rare indeed that Māra Pāpīyān, upon hearing this sutra being preached, does not create obstacles.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is because he has not heard it that he does not create obstacles."

"Why is this? It is because the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, by means of his supernormal powers, concealed [the sound] so that it could not be heard; therefore, there was no obstruction. At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī withdrew his supernormal powers.

Immediately, the evil Māra Pāpīyān, while still in his dream, heard the preaching of the unprecedented and marvelous wheel of the non-retrogressive Dharma, and he also heard the name of Śākyamuni Buddha being invoked. He was instantly startled awake, filled with grief, anxiety, and terror such that the hairs on his body stood on end. He threw himself from his bed onto the ground and spoke these words:
"That which was previously subdued no longer submits to me; that territory formerly under my command no longer belongs to me.

Distressed, sorrowful, and afflicted, he broke into loud weeping. Because of this distress, sorrow, and affliction expressed through loud weeping, his body became aged and emaciated, like that of a man a hundred years old.
At that time, the evil Māra Pāpīyān, leading his fourfold army and all the māra-devas of the trichiliocosm, came to where the Buddha was;
it was just as when a bodhisattva sits beneath the tree of enlightenment, and the māras array their troops and come to where the Buddha is—so too was this.

At that time, the evil Māra Pāpīyān assumed a physical form as decrepit as that of a hundred-year-old man; his head was bowed, his spine was hunched, his gait was slow and heavy, he gasped for breath, his entire body trembled, and he approached the Buddha’s dwelling leaning upon a staff.
When Māra Pāpīyas came before the Buddha, his retinue of fourfold armies in the air heard the preaching of the irreversible Dharma-wheel and also heard the name of Śākyamuni Buddha.
At that time, the fourfold army and its retinue stood still of their own accord, unable to advance, and gave rise to this thought:
"We shall no longer follow Pāpīyān."
At that time, Pāpīyas was alone, emaciated, and aged; he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Not even a single person remains to support me. Those whom I formerly subdued do not submit to me now, and the territories I previously governed no longer belong to me."

"The World-Honored One has compassion for all sentient beings; yet I am now among the number of those sentient beings, and he does not extend his compassion to me, nor has he left even a single person to give me water."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pāpīyas, saying:
"The realm of sentient beings is vast and is of an inexhaustible nature.
Pāpīyas, you should know this!"

Even if, day after day, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to appear in the world, and each of those Buddhas were to deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges into parinirvāṇa every single day, the realm of sentient beings would still never be exhausted.
Then Māra Pāpīyas again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Although the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, I am now alone, weak, and old; if I were to stumble or fall while traveling on the road, there would be no one at all to support or receive me.”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will comfort my mind, so that I may depart in joy and return quickly.
The Buddha told Pāpīyas:

"Set your mind at ease and depart. If there are sentient beings who do not have faith, do not understand, and do not regress from the Dharma, all such beings belong to you; they are your kin, over whom you have mastery, and all are your supporters."
At that time, having heard these words, Pāpīyān leapt for joy and spoke thus:

"I shall now create various obstacles for sentient beings, causing them to lack faith and understanding regarding this Dharma and to give rise to doubt and confusion. Because they give rise to doubt and confusion, they shall come under my influence, and I shall attain mastery over them."
At that time, Pāpīyas again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will once more comfort me, so that I may depart with joy.
For the Buddha himself has said:"
"If there are sentient beings who hear my name, they shall all never regress from Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
From this day forward, do not speak of this again.
"Why is this? Because if there are sentient beings who, having heard these words, shall practice with diligent vigor in their quest for the Bodhi of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pāpīyan, saying:
“Go with a peaceful mind!

I shall cause all sentient beings to reach a state where there is not even one who dwells in bodhi, nor any who depart from the realm of sentient beings; there shall be no sentient being who departs from the aggregate of form, nor any who departs from the aggregates of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”

Pāpīyān, rest assured and depart! I shall always ensure that all sentient beings are free from the view of a self-body; free from attachment to precepts and attachment to views; free from those who grasp at attainments; free from the sixty-two views; free from perceptions of the past, future, and present; free from killing; free from taking what is not given and sexual misconduct; free from false speech, frivolous speech, harsh speech, and divisive speech; and free from covetousness, malice, and wrong views.
Pāpīyān, you may depart in peace!

I do not instruct sentient beings to practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom; nor do I instruct sentient beings to practice the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). I do not cause sentient beings to abandon the notion of "sentient being," the notion of "solid attachment," the notion of "parents," the notions of "brothers, sisters, sons, or daughters," the notion of "day and night," the notions of "half-month, month, or year," the notions of "giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom," the notion of "the thought of enlightenment" (*bodhicitta*), the notions of "powers" (*bala*) and "fearlessnesses" (*vaiśāradya*), the notions of "faculties, powers, factors of awakening, or the path," the notions of "Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha," the notion of "obstacles to enlightenment," or the notion of "omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Pāpīyān, you may now depart with a peaceful mind!
I shall cause sentient beings to have no perception of distance from any dharma.

At that time, Pāpīyān was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he extracted the arrows of sorrow and anxiety, and immediately at that spot restored his original form. He scattered various heavenly flowers over the Buddha, circumambulated the Buddha three times, stood before him, and spoke these verses:
"Today the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings Has uttered this subtle and wondrous sound;
The Buddha has no double-tongued speech, And now I am filled with great joy.

When Māra Pāpīyas had spoken these verses, he was joyful and composed in mind; he gradually departed from the Buddha and returned to his own celestial palace, where all the devas gathered together. There they enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses to amuse themselves, and never again gave rise to the intent to create obstacles.
When this teaching on the subduing and expulsion of māras was spoken, the great earth shook in six ways.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"For what cause and condition does the great earth tremble?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"When this Dharma for subduing and expelling Māra was being taught, sixty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) regarding all phenomena."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is there anyone present in this assembly who harbors doubts regarding this Dharma?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In this assembly today, there are ten billion sentient beings who have all given rise to doubt and confusion, their minds distressed, and they speak thus:
'What kind of words are these? Could it be that we have heard them erroneously?'"

Because of these circumstances, they did not know the time or the direction; nor did they know from where they had come or where they were going. Due to their confusion, they could not see one another.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:

“I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of a heart of compassion, will swiftly provide illumination for these sentient beings, so that this assembly does not fall into the evil realms due to harboring doubts and confusion.”
For what reason do you say this:
"O Evil Māra Pāpīyān, go now in peace!
I shall not cause sentient beings to abide in bodhi; even until then, O Pāpīyān, go in peace!"?
"I do not cause sentient beings to have the notion of non-detachment from all phenomena.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will swiftly provide illumination for these sentient beings, and so that future sentient beings may also attain this illumination; having received and upheld this Dharma without forgetting it, I pray that you will explain it in detail.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Awakening has no characteristic of abiding, Nor is there anyone who can abide in it;
Therefore, it is said of sentient beings That none abide in awakening.”
Bodhi and sentient beings are non-dual and without distinction;
therefore it is said that among sentient beings there is no one who dwells in bodhi.
Nor is there any sentient being who can depart from the realm of sentient beings.
Non-existent and unarisen, it is ultimately unattainable.
The inconceivable realm of sentient beings is by nature empty from the beginning;
even if one possessed all-knowledge, one would not perceive it as being apart from conceptualization.
The aggregates I have taught cannot be separated from sentient beings;
these aggregates and sentient beings are no different, being equally quiescent and extinguished.
Knowing that the aggregates are empty, yet not departing from their nature.
It is taught that their essence is one, Neither to be grasped nor to be abandoned.
Having understood the aggregates (*skandhas*) thus, One neither grasps them nor abandons them;
Being without self and without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), They ultimately have nothing upon which to rely.
The aggregates are like space, and the activity of the aggregates is likewise;
because there is no activity in their activity, the aggregates are said to be like space.
Just as the realm of space is said to be neither born nor capable of giving birth, so too are the aggregates.
The same applies to the female gender; there is no one who can be separated from it.
The self-nature and characteristics of the view of a self are dharmas that cannot be apprehended;
because they cannot be apprehended, I say they cannot be separated from.
Doubt has no intrinsic nature; it is ultimately unfindable.
Because doubt cannot be found, there are no sentient beings who can be separated from it.
There are no sentient beings capable of maintaining the precepts of discernment.
Those sentient beings who grasp at views are likewise unobtainable.
One who calculates that there is a "grasper of dharmas" cannot find such a sentient being;
yet the mind that grasps at dharmas does not exist apart from its own nature.
As for the various views that have been taught, there are sixty-two in total;
all such views are like reflections in water.
Having understood that these various views are all like reflections in water;
Without self and without anything belonging to a self, their intrinsic nature is unattainable.
Perceptions of the past and future, as well as perceptions of the present—these perceptions have no existence; they are like reflections in water.
This perception is devoid of self; sentient beings cannot be found.
Because sentient beings cannot be found, they cannot be separated from [the state of non-existence].
To kill and harm sentient beings will inevitably lead one to perilous and evil realms.
Established within nirvāṇa, there is nothing that can move them.
If sentient beings were obtainable, there could be the characteristic of being free from movement;
since sentient beings have no reality, it is said they cannot be separated [from it].
Enlightenment is called "non-giving," for there has never been one who gives it;
though one may diligently employ skillful means, there is no shifting away from it.
One does not bestow gifts upon sentient beings, but teaches them to practice the supreme gift of Dharma.
Though one diligently applies skillful means, there is nothing that can be moved or separated.
Furthermore, no sentient being is found who relies upon sensual desire;
within desire there is no "wrong" that could be joined with what is not wrong.
For those sentient beings who speak falsely, one should manifest through skillful means;
yet though one exerts diligent effort, there is no one who can cause them to move or depart.
This applies to those who engage in divisive speech, harsh words, and untimely talk.
Such verbal expressions as these are like echoes that delude people.
These phenomena have no location and cannot be stained by attachment;
these various sounds are like echoes, known to have no basis.
The ignorance inherent within oneself is deeply attached to a self;
yet once the true nature of the self is known, nothing can cause one to waver or depart from it.
One can likewise know that anger is ultimately devoid of any intrinsic characteristic.
Because awakening is signless, there is nothing that can move or depart from it.
If one can understand false views, this is called right view;
by transcending attachment to dharmas of view, there is nothing that can move or depart from it.
Not to teach sentient beings, yet to give them women’s forms;
this is what the worthy and holy ones prohibit—for such giving brings with it faults and calamities.
Precepts maintained out of false views are cast aside by the Path of the Sages.
The wise should not teach that one seeks the noble Dharma by means of these various marks of forbearance praised by the non-Buddhists;
such forbearance is not the right path that leads a person to Nirvāṇa.
The five-fold austerity practiced by the non-Buddhists, though praised by them, cannot lead to enlightenment; the wise should abandon it.
All the meditative concentrations of the non-Buddhists involve the conceptualization of existence.
Not praised by the Buddhas, they therefore do not teach others;
using only worldly wisdom, they seek to transform sentient beings,
yet with this wisdom they cannot attain the inconceivable wisdom of the Buddhas.
Regarding those pure beings who have attained fearlessness,
I say that for such a multitude, the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are not to be practiced.
For those who deeply revere and mindfully recollect the Buddha, I do not teach them to abandon this attachment.
The Buddha possesses untainted wisdom and is likewise free from all obstacles.
For one who deeply reveres and contemplates the Dharma, he does not teach the abandoning of such attachment;
for how could the supreme Dharma of detachment itself be abandoned?
Without clinging to the notion of sentient beings, one gives rise to the bodhicitta;
since bodhi itself is not to be clung to, how could it be otherwise?
One should likewise abandon notions of parents, brothers, sisters, sons, and daughters.
These perceptions are all like illusions; how can they be abandoned?
These perceptions exist everywhere, yet there is no phenomenon and nothing exists;
because there is no phenomenon and nothing exists, how can they be abandoned?
The perception of day and the perception of night, the perception of half-months and months—
these perceptions lack reality, like water in a mirage during the heat.
The perception of giving and the perception of precepts, the perception of patience and the perception of diligence;
This perception is not a true perception; how, then, can one be liberated through perception?

The perception of meditative concentration, the perception of wisdom, and the perception of the bodhicitta—these perceptions, as well as those of the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the faculties, are all false and deceptive.
The notions of the various factors of awakening and the path, the notion of the Buddha and the notion of the Dharma—all these arise from ignorance; how can one be free from such notions?
One discriminates the notion of the Sangha, and these notions are likewise manifold.
Because it arises from conceptual discrimination, I say it cannot be abandoned.
To be attached to the notion of awakening, as well as the notion of omniscience—
such notions distance one from all Buddhas and from inconceivable awakening.
For this reason I say: Pāpīyān is a man without wisdom;
not free from these various conceptualizations, he seeks awakening far away.
All phenomena and awakening are known entirely as suchness (tathatā).
"Proclaiming the meaning of non-separation, He removes the demons' hearts of sorrow and affliction.

When the World-Honored One definitively preached this Dharma for subduing and expelling demons, ten billion sentient beings within the assembly extracted the arrows of hesitation; they were no longer subject to doubt, attained great illumination, and realized the patience of the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Ten billion sentient beings within the assembly all gathered together in harmony before the Buddha and spoke these verses:
"The inconceivable path of the Buddha, We have now realized and known through direct experience;
The Buddha is the teacher who guides the world, Who has severed and eliminated our doubts."
Having attained great illumination, they dwell securely within the Buddha-dharma;
because all directions are bright and pure, they are able to see ten million buddhas.
They also perceive their teachings and realize that form and other phenomena are unarisen.
Having encountered the Teacher who saves the world, one attains such pure wisdom as this;
one also beholds ten million Buddhas and their adorned, pure lands,
with all those supreme guides of the world dwelling therein.

At that time, after these ten billion sentient beings had spoken this verse, they removed the exquisite robes they were wearing and, out of joy in making offerings to the Dharma, reverently presented them to the Buddha, saying:
"We pray that this Dharma may spread so that all sentient beings may hear it."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this Dharma for subduing and expelling Māra, are able to believe and understand it without giving rise to doubt or confusion, how much merit will these good sons and good daughters obtain?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“If any son or daughter of good family, upon hearing this Dharma for subduing and expelling māras, can believe and understand it after it passes through their ears once, without harboring doubt, their merit will be exceedingly great and immeasurable.”
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Can the merit thus obtained be known through comparison or analogy?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to make offerings to a hundred thousand Buddhas during the first part of the day, to a hundred thousand Buddhas during the middle part of the day, and to a hundred thousand Buddhas during the latter part of the day—honoring and praising them, providing them with excellent dwellings and all necessities in full abundance—for the course of a hundred thousand kalpas, would the merit obtained by that son or daughter of good family be great?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is exceedingly much, exceedingly much; it is immeasurable and difficult to know through analogy.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If a son or daughter of good family, upon hearing this Dharma for subduing and expelling māras, can believe and understand it after it has passed through their ears once, without harboring doubt, their merit shall surpass that of the former."

At that time, three sons of good family seeking the Bodhisattva vehicle appeared spontaneously in the midst of space and gradually approached. Each held a thousand great lotus flowers; these flowers were so high and broad they surpassed Mount Sumeru, possessing hundreds of thousands of millions of petals that emitted hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light in various colors.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda and all those present in the assembly together saw from afar three sons of good family seeking the Bodhisattva vehicle approaching gradually; having seen them, they were struck with a sense of wonder.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
From where has this good man come?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"To the east, past buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a world named Flower-High Sumeru. This son of good family has come because he heard this Dharma and these aforementioned causes and conditions being taught in that world."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha,
“What is the name of the Buddha in that world?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“That Buddha is named Sumerukūṭarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and he currently dwells there preaching the Dharma.

At that time, those three sons of good family who sought the Bodhisattva vehicle went before Śākyamuni Buddha; they prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with single-minded devotion joined their palms. Taking the flowers they held, they scattered them over the Buddha and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!...”
We are now able to believe and understand this Dharma, giving rise to no doubt or hesitation. Why is this?
Because within this Dharma, we are free from doubt and uncertainty, just like the Tathāgata.
At that time, the foremost son of good family who sought the Bodhisattva vehicle addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If it is said as follows:”
"I am the Tathāgata"—
this statement is indeed the correct teaching. Why is this so?
"Because I have not given rise to doubt or confusion regarding this Dharma.
At that time, the second son of good family, who sought the Bodhisattva vehicle, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If one were to say,
"I am the World-Honored One," this statement would indeed be a correct one.
"Why is this? It is because I have given rise to no doubt or confusion regarding this Dharma.
At that time, the third son of good family, who sought the Bodhisattva vehicle, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one were to say:
‘I am the Buddha.’”
"These words are indeed the correct teaching.
Why is this? Because I have given rise to no doubt or uncertainty regarding this Dharma."
At that time, the minds of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in the assembly were all agitated and unsettled in their seats, and they thought to themselves:
"There are never two Buddhas appearing simultaneously in the world; for what reason has this son of good family spoken such words?"
Having had this thought, they spoke to one another in turn:
"Let us remain silent for now;
since the World-Honored One is seated here, he himself shall explain the meaning of these words spoken by these bodhisattvas."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the names of these bodhisattvas?”
"Only then can one let out this great lion's roar.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"The first bodhisattva is named Seeking the Sound of the Tathāgata; the second bodhisattva is named Seeking the Sound of the World-Honored One; the third bodhisattva is named Seeking the Sound of the Buddha."
“Ānanda, you should know that for this reason, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas speak in such a manner.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In this assembly there are now hundreds of thousands of sentient beings whose minds are all agitated, and they think thus:
‘There are not two Buddhas appearing simultaneously in the world; for what reason does he speak these words?’”

"I only pray that the Tathāgata will expound upon its meaning, so that the minds of this great assembly shall not be disturbed, and the roots of goodness they have planted may increase and become bright and pure.
World-Honored One!"

It is like a person who has bathed and groomed their hair, nails, and complexion until they are bright and pure; if they were then to bathe their body again with red sandalwood water, their complexion would become even more bright and pure than before.
World-Honored One!
These sentient beings are likewise; if they hear this explanation of the meaning of these words, the roots of goodness they have planted will increase, becoming more brilliant and pure than before.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Listen all with one mind as I explain the meaning of these words:
For what reason is he called the Tathāgata, The World-Honored One, and the Buddha?”
Able to know the suchness of the past, And likewise knowing the suchness of the future;
Seeing the suchness of all phenomena— For this reason, he is called the Tathāgata.
Just as the Buddhas of former times Practiced inconceivable giving;
I, too, have practiced this giving; it is for this reason that I speak thus.
Just as the Buddhas of former times sought the path free from dependence, I likewise seek it; therefore, I am called the Tathāgata.
Not dwelling in any phenomena, he seeks the tranquil bodhi;
yet even bodhi is not attained—therefore he is called the Tathāgata.
Just as the bodhisattvas of old diligently practiced asceticism and patience;
I, too, have practiced this patience, and am thus able to reach the further shore of patience.
Just as I formerly exerted myself with diligence in my quest for bodhi, so too has he exerted himself with diligent effort; for this reason, he is called the Tathāgata.
Having already attained thorough penetration of the equal nature of all phenomena, he does not give rise to mental conceptions;
for this reason, he is called the Tathāgata.
He does not dwell upon any phenomena, for their nature is eternally equal.
Having realized this equality, one is free from a mind of discrimination.
Having attained mastery over this samādhi of suchness-equality,
and because of having mastered this samādhi, one is therefore called a Tathāgata.
All dharmas that have been taught each possess their own specific nature and characteristics;
having known these natures and characteristics, they are ultimately and eternally quiescent.
To know these characteristics is called wisdom (*prajñā*); to know their emptiness is called knowledge (*jñāna*).
If one can know sentient beings, one is said to have reached the further shore of wisdom.
Just as the wise ones of old reached the further shore through wisdom,
so too, by not grasping at this wisdom, one reaches the further shore in profound stillness.
He too has attained this wisdom and reached the other shore;
because he has attained this wisdom, he is therefore called the Tathāgata.
He has not attained a "Bodhi-tathatā" (suchness of enlightenment), for its nature and characteristics are difficult to discuss.
Not grasping any dharma, for this reason he is called the Tathāgata.
Having already attained non-attachment, he does not cling even to suchness as a Tathāgata;
because he has penetrated the path of non-attachment, he does not cling to any dharma.
Like the Teacher who guides the world, he is able to know and see the right path;
this path’s true nature has never had beginning or end.
He likewise cultivates in this way the most excellent, unsurpassed path.
This path has no beginning and no end; its nature is empty and devoid of existence.
Knowing that the path has no beginning or end, one knows that all phenomena are equal;
knowing also that they are like [space] in their equality, for this reason one is called the Tathāgata.
The Way is like the suchness of bodhi, And likewise the suchness of non-abiding;
Knowing suchness to be like empty space, For this reason he is called the Tathāgata.
All dharmas that I have taught Are eternally equal in their suchness.
If one can perceive this suchness, one should seek awakening.
Ānanda, for this reason, he spoke thus;
as he has spoken, so can he practice, and as he has spoken, so does he act.
If one can practice this conduct and can speak in such a manner,
know that these are the fearless Bodhisattvas who have reached the stage of non-retrogression.
Ānanda, you should know them as the fearless Bodhisattvas.
"One who can speak in such a way may truly say of themselves: 'I am the Tathāgata.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"By what causes and conditions, and by attaining what dharma, is one named 'World-Honored One' (Bhagavān)?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"All listen with a single mind: Throughout hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas..."
Seeking such enlightenment, immeasurable and inconceivable,
for the sake of all sentient beings, one seeks such enlightenment;
never having any fear, for this reason one is called the World-Honored One.
Not fearing birth and death, dwelling rightly within birth and death;
transforming and delivering all sentient beings—for this reason he is called the World-Honored One.
Why is there no fear?
How does one dwell in birth and death?
How does one deliver sentient beings?
Why is one called the World-Honored One?
In birth and death there is no dharma that can be destroyed;
being neither solid nor destructible, by this one delivers sentient beings.
This is called fearlessness; this is called abiding in birth and death.
This is called delivering sentient beings; this is called the World-Honored One.
Knowing that all phenomena are empty, he possesses no timid or weak mind;
he proclaims the characteristics of all phenomena without any fear.
Having severed all fears, he has distanced himself from all places of peril;
because he does not fear such perilous places, he delivers sentient beings from them.
He delivers many billions of sentient beings, leading them across the treacherous difficulties of birth and death.
Neither birth-and-death nor the sentient beings to be delivered can be apprehended;
yet all sentient beings are established upon the shore of tranquil nirvana.
Since no sentient being can be apprehended either, this is what is called the World-Honored One.
Constantly for the sake of all sentient beings, He preaches the Dharma which is like space;
Never giving rise to fear— Such a one is called the World-Honored One.
The nature of phenomena has no differentiation, Yet he speaks of it by various names.
Equal as bodhi, bodhi cannot be apprehended.
He instructs all sentient beings, causing them to incline toward bodhi;
though he teaches such a Dharma, he has never said anything at all.
Speaking that which is unspeakable, you deliver and liberate many sentient beings;
fearless and without grasping, for this reason you are called the World-Honored One.
Having distanced yourself from all conceptualizations, you are able to cultivate the marks of Bodhi.
Having transcended all perceptions, he is called the World-Honored One.
Having been able to extinguish all perceptions, afflictions remain none;
for this reason he receives the title and is named the World-Honored One.
Observing all phenomena with wisdom, one knows that all phenomena are equal;
never seeking even the slightest phenomenon, for this reason he is called the World-Honored One.
He does not value reputation, nor does he seek reputation.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they constantly teach the Dharma that is free from fame.
Awakening is free from fame; they seek it in that very same way.
If one values fame and reputation, this is called being far from awakening.
This sound is like an echo; through conceptualization, it becomes manifold.
One falsely gives rise to various discriminations, thinking, "I have such a name.
Do not cling to any sounds, nor rely upon names.
Enlightenment is free from conceptual proliferation; this is what is called the World-Honored One.
Knowing all such phenomena is what is called the World-Honored One;
furthermore, since enlightenment itself cannot be apprehended, he is therefore named the World-Honored One.
Knowing all such phenomena, yet having nothing to which one is attached;
seeking such enlightenment, one attains liberation free from outflows. Ānanda!
"For these reasons, and for other causes and conditions,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva declares himself to be the World-Honored One.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions, and by attaining what dharma, is one named a Buddha?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Awakened to all phenomena, yet realizing these phenomena are non-existent;
having awakened to the non-existence of phenomena, he is therefore called a Buddha.
Having fully understood all afflictions, he does not allow them to gain mastery."
Through wisdom one is detached from afflictions; for this reason, one is called a Buddha.
One is able to realize that this body is empty and that this body belongs to nothing;
this body is not solid, for solidity cannot be found.
Fools conceive a notion of solidity regarding this fragile body;
he who realizes it as it truly is is therefore called a Buddha.
Having awakened to the fact that ignorance and lack of wisdom have no inherent nature, he is free from them.
Having already attained clear wisdom, he is therefore called a Buddha.
All past perceptions he awakens to as being without perception;
because he knows that perception is signless, he no longer follows after such signs.
Cultivating all future perceptions, and likewise those of the present;
having cultivated all perceptions, for this reason he is called a Buddha.
He realizes that the prior limit of form has never arisen.
Although the various minor [perceptions] are discriminated, they cannot cause form to arise.
Sensation has no fundamental basis; its basis cannot be found.
Within all phenomena, there is likewise no experiencer of sensation.
Knowing that perception is like an illusion, its nature being non-existent;
among all phenomena, one is not entangled by perception.
Knowing that cognition cannot produce the various marks of the body, [one is liberated].
The body is empty and its activity is also empty; therefore, there is nothing to be done.
Knowing that both activity and the body are like the plantain tree, one who can realize this as it truly is is therefore called a Buddha.
Contemplating the true nature of consciousness, it is not found within the body;
nor is it found outside the body, yet this consciousness exists.
Within all phenomena, the nature of consciousness cannot be apprehended.
Within this body, there is no form and no location.
One who can understand consciousness in this way realizes that the nature of consciousness is non-existent;
it is without conceptualization, like an illusion, and its arising has never been seen.
Among all phenomena, there is no one who perceives or cognizes them;
the nature of all sentient beings has never had a creator.
Since sentient beings have no creator, all phenomena are ultimately perfected and complete.
Whether phenomena or sentient beings, there is no characteristic of coming or going.
Awakening to all phenomena as ultimately devoid of characteristics,
free from conceptual discrimination and idle proliferation— for this reason, one is called a Buddha.
Just as the Buddhas do not abide in the Buddha’s True Dharma, the Mahāyāna;
they do not abide in any phenomena, and for this reason they are called Buddhas.
Just as all phenomena are suchness (tathatā), the Buddhas do not abide in suchness.
The Buddha is like bodhi; ultimately, neither can be apprehended.
For the sake of seeking bodhi, one should give rise to such a mind;
yet, being able to awaken to the characteristics of this mind, not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended.
For the sake of seeking awakening, one should give rise to such a mind;
this mind and awakening are equal, and one should likewise realize they are like an illusion. Ānanda!
For these reasons, they speak in this manner;
they claim for themselves, "I am a Buddha," like the Buddhas who guide the world as teachers.
Using the name and reputation of a Buddha, they preach such teachings as these.
If there are those who abide in this Dharma, they should all seek awakening.
If there are those who understand this Dharma, they are then close to awakening;
regarding all phenomena, they give rise to no doubts whatsoever.
"Free from doubt regarding all dharmas, one will surely become supreme in the world;
because one has already known this dharma, one is able to decipher the meaning of the secret words.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken the names of the Tathāgatas, World-Honored Buddhas, hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in the assembly addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We are no longer entangled in the net of doubt and have attained great illumination. We have understood the meaning of the names ‘Tathāgata,’ ‘World-Honored One,’ and ‘Buddha’ for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; because all dharmas are unobtainable, we have attained the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*) within all phenomena.”

The Tathāgata now treats us with compassion as a parent would, not allowing our minds to be disturbed, and enabling us to realize the undisturbed nature of phenomena, which is like space and cannot be disturbed.
"Why is this? Because we have now realized that all dharmas are like space, being without agitation.

At that time, hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in the assembly prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and sat silently not far from the Buddha.

At that time, there was in the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Constantly Laughing with Pure Faculties (*Sadāhasita-viśuddhendriya*). He rose from his seat, scattered various flowers over the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
“Sentient beings have many conceptions of fruits; One who can dissolve those conceptions of fruits, Having abandoned fruit to attain fulfillment— To him, the World-Knower, I pay homage.”
Sentient beings are greedily attached to fruits and engage in various activities for the sake of such fruits;
only the Buddha can remove and explain this, and thus we pay homage to the World-Knower.
He proclaims the equality of all fruits and awakens others thereby.
You teach that fruits are merely provisional names; therefore, I pay homage to the World-Knower.
You proclaim the Dharma of equality and abide within the Dharma of equality;
you awaken to the equality of all phenomena; therefore, I pay homage to the World-Knower.
Sentient beings conceive the notion of attaining fruits;
to eliminate this mind that clings to attainment, only a Buddha can sever it completely; therefore, I pay homage to the World-Knower.
Fully knowing that the fruit is quiescent cessation, he does not dwell in various fruits.
"The Buddhas possess excellent secret speech; therefore, I pay homage to the World-Knower.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Constantly Smiling with Pure Faculties, having spoken this verse, praised the World-Honored One, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him three times to the right. Not far from the Buddha, he gazed at the Buddha with single-minded devotion, his eyes not blinking for a moment, remaining there in joyful composure.
At that time, there was in the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Padmaguṇagarbha. He rose from his seat, scattered flowers over the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
“Sentient beings possess many conceptions, yet they are able to understand this mind;
Free from fear and grasping at nothing, I therefore pay homage to the Honored Muni.”
Regarding the tranquility of all existence, you teach the Dharma of non-existence;
because you have transcended all forms of being, I pay homage to the Honored Muni.
Knowing that existence is empty and void, its nature is devoid of a self.
Because he is far removed from fear, I pay homage to the Honored Muni.
Because he is far removed from all sorrows and grief, and is able to uproot sorrow and grief;
Because he has forever severed all fetters, I pay homage to the Honored Muni.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Padmaguṇagañja, having spoken these verses, praised the World-Honored One and further spoke in verse,
addressing the Buddha: "In the evil ages of the future, if there be those who hear this sutra and do not give rise to fear,
they all should join their palms in prostration."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalamati, before the Buddha, spoke these verses:
"If there are those who hear this sutra And do not give rise to doubt or confusion,
At all times, they should scatter various flowers [upon them]."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vistīrṇamati spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“In this sūtra, the immeasurable dharmas of all Buddhas are extensively expounded;
among sentient beings who hear these teachings, few are without doubt.”
Attached to their own bodies, they give rise to various conceptions of self;
upon hearing such a sutra as this, they claim it is a perverted teaching.
Know that such persons belong to Māra and are held fast by Māra.
Those lacking wisdom, upon hearing this sutra, will instead give rise to further doubt and confusion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Blue Lotus Eye spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“If there are those who hear this sutra and do not give rise to doubt or confusion;”
"He is like the eye of the world, and is also called the Giver of Eyes.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Delight-in-Worship-of-Stūpas spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"If there are those who hear this sutra and give rise to deep faith and joy;
"This person dwelling in the world is like the most supreme stūpa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ke-yang-i (Thirsting-with-Longing-Mind) spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"Though remaining within the cycle of birth and death, one should repeatedly give rise to thirsting-longing;
"Not clinging to any phenomena, one can be free from doubt regarding this sutra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Delight-in-Giving-Clothing spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"One should offer many billions of garments, fine, soft, and even;
"To provide for the covering of his body, one must not doubt this Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Delight-in-Giving-Sacrifice spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"Of all the various delicacies mentioned, those with the most excellent flavors;"
"One should provide for such a person who does not doubt this Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Karuṇāmukha, out of compassion for sentient beings, spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"One should weep again and again, out of compassion for all sentient beings."
Yet within this sutra, they lack any inclination of faith or joy.
If a person, for even a brief moment, harbors doubt regarding this sutra,
know that they have come from hell and shall return once more toward hell.
Associating with evil companions, they do not understand this profound Dharma;
shrouded by the net of ignorance, they do not turn toward this wondrous destination.
Bound and entangled by their own broken precepts, they harbor malicious intent and delight in seeking out the faults of others.
Attached to gain and offerings, they will be able to slander this sutra;
not diligently seeking awakening, they are indolent and lack vigor;
possessing evil wisdom and delighting in inferior teachings, they do not believe or understand this sutra.
Sentient beings who crave gain and offerings, who conceive of a self and follow their desires;
those deeply attached to the three periods of time, cannot believe in this sutra.
Those of foolish, perverse, and evil nature, stained by craving, blind and without wisdom;
Those who delight in idle talk and do not believe this sutra;
those who are fond of selecting fine clothes and greedy for flavors and food;
those with little of the pure Dharma—these are able to slander this sutra.
Sentient beings who have attained the fruit delight in preaching the Dharma of the fruit;
those who can understand the Buddha’s subtle and secret words are exceedingly rare.
In ages past, there were Buddhas, the unsurpassed guides and teachers of the world.
"Those who are able to make offerings in full, are able to have faith and understanding in this sutra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Far-removed-from-Evil-Dharmas (Pāpadharma-vivikta) spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"The foolish mind greedily clings to fruits, and is thus able to slander this sutra;
One should keep far from such a person, Just as one avoids stinking excrement and filth,
Or like a rotting corpse, Which all practitioners avoid from afar;
Sentient beings who slander this sutra Should always be kept at a distance.
Just as when bandits plundering a village dwell in a vast wilderness,
and all who hear of them flee in haste, fearing they will bring them trouble—
so too should one flee, staying far away from these evil thieves.
"Those who harbor malice and ill will, and slander this sutra.
*The Sutra of the Vast, Pure, and Unregressing Wheel*, Volume Five, Spoken by the Buddha.
*The Sutra of the Vast, Pure, and Unregressing Wheel*, Volume [Five].
Translated by the śramaṇa Zhìyán of Liangzhou during the Song dynasty.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is truly rare that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have so decisively and skillfully expounded the Dharma of bodhi.
World-Honored One!”
"Is this due to the power of this samādhi, or is it due to the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, or is it due to the power of the samādhi within this sutra that enables such a teaching?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"These sons of good family have, in the past, heard this sutra being taught by sixty billion nayutas of Buddhas without any increase or decrease; it is exactly like the subtle and secret words I speak now, identical and without difference."
He was not able to make such a statement by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Why is this?
Because he has directly perceived and thoroughly realized this sūtra.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are those who, upon hearing this sutra, are able to believe and understand it, giving rise to no doubt or confusion.”
“World-Honored One!
How much merit will these sons and daughters of good family obtain?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family desires to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and offers as much of the seven treasures as would fill Jambudvīpa to all the Tathāgatas—yet if there is another son of good family or daughter of good family who, upon hearing this sutra, believes, understands, and does not doubt it, Ānanda, you should know this! "
The merit obtained from this is exceedingly great, exceedingly great. Ānanda!

Setting aside Jambudvīpa, suppose one were to fill worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with the seven treasures and offer them to all the Tathāgatas; yet if there should be someone who hears this sutra and believes, understands, and does not doubt it, their merit would surpass that of the former.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one were to take the Jambudvīpa world, Filled with the seven kinds of precious jewels, And offer them to all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, Those who guide the world with compassion; "
Furthermore, if one were to take as many precious jewels as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
filling worlds as numerous as those very sands, and offer them all to the Buddhas;
yet if there should be someone who hears this sutra and is able to believe and understand it— [the latter’s merit would be far greater].
"Nor will they give rise to doubt; their merit shall surpass that [of the former].
At that time, Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"

If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this sutra, are able to believe and understand it; and having believed and understood it, further receive, uphold, read, recite, and master it—how much merit will these good sons and good daughters obtain?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, were to distance themselves from this sūtra and practice the dāna-pāramitā by making offerings to the Buddhas for a hundred kalpas; and likewise, for a hundred kalpas, were to maintain the precepts, practice patience, exert diligence, cultivate meditative concentration, give rise to the five supernatural powers, and practice wisdom—because they have distanced themselves from this sūtra, their merit would not equal that of a son or daughter of good family who hears this sūtra, believes and understands it without doubt, and receives, upholds, reads, recites, and masters it thoroughly; the latter’s merit surpasses the former.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "If,
throughout a full hundred kalpas, One were to provide various delicacies To the Teacher who guides the world,
It would not yet be called making an offering to the Buddha."
If one can uphold this sutra, this is called making offerings to the Buddha;
because all Buddhas revere the Dharma, this is the unsurpassed form of reverence.
Even if one were to scatter various kinds of robes throughout a full hundred kalpas;
The Greatly Diligent Savior, who has not yet been named as a Buddha worthy of offerings—
if one can uphold this sutra, this is the most supreme offering;
this is what is called making an offering to the Buddha, surpassing the previous gift of robes.
If, throughout a full hundred eons, one were to scatter various flowers upon the Greatly Diligent Savior of the World,
it would not yet be called making an offering to a Buddha.
Those who wish to make the most supreme offering to all Buddhas [should practice as follows].
One should uphold this sutra, remaining unstained by and unattached to any fruits of merit.
This offering is the great offering, the most supreme among all offerings;
if one can uphold this sutra, they will not harbor notions of a self.
If one were to steadfastly maintain pure precepts for a full hundred kalpas,
yet did not uphold this sutra, those would all lack renown;
but if one can uphold this sutra, these precepts will possess renown.
Among all precepts, this is supreme; it excels the prior practice of giving and morality.
Though one may possess pure and stainless precepts, immeasurable and inconceivable, one should always diligently seek to receive and uphold a sūtra such as this.
As it is said in this sutra: one who practices the precepts well is neither called one of evil precepts nor one who has broken the precepts.
If one upholds the precepts of this sutra, they are called those who uphold the bodhicitta precepts.
Maintaining the precepts of bodhi-samādhi, One is fully endowed with the unconditioned precepts.
All such precepts as these Are all expounded in this sutra;
If one can uphold this sutra, One will be fully endowed with all precepts.
If a person were to practice great patience for a full hundred kalpas,
enduring all the insults and abuse of sentient beings with a mind capable of forbearance;
and even if their hands and feet were severed, their body would remain unmoved and undisturbed.
Never having given rise to an evil mind, One does not harbor anger or resentment toward others.
Practicing such patience as that of the Rishi Kṣāntivādin,
Even if one were to do so for a hundred kalpas, That patience would not be considered supreme.
If there are those who hear this sutra, Who believe, understand, and can endure it;
This patience is called supreme, This patience is called noble and good.
This patience is called most excellent, This patience is unsurpassed.
If one can uphold this sutra without any defilement or attachment,
and seeks the undefiled, unsurpassed wisdom of all Buddhas,
one should not give rise to attachment; quickly receive and uphold this sutra.
If for a full hundred eons one were to stand constantly without sitting or lying down,
casting off all sleep and practicing great diligence;
if the wise person applies diligent effort to propagate such a sūtra as this—
This person attains fearlessness, surpassing those of great diligence;
even if they were to manifest the five supernormal powers throughout a full hundred kalpas,
if they do not hear this sutra, their wisdom shall not be supreme.
If one can uphold this sutra and penetrate the meaning of non-reliance,
among all supernormal powers, this power is the most supreme.
Even if one were to practice all forms of wisdom for a full hundred kalpas, [it would not equal this].
This wisdom is worldly, for it discriminates worldly phenomena.
If one does not study this sutra, one cannot be called possessed of clear wisdom;
if one can study this sutra, that is called firm wisdom.
If there are those who hear this sutra and possess unsurpassed faith and joy,
such persons are called wise and are also called those who have attained thorough penetration.
With such wisdom, they are able to know the suchness of all phenomena.
One should proclaim this sutra, and thus one shall attain such wisdom.
The dharmas practiced by the wise are all expounded within this sutra;
one should apply oneself with diligent vigor to receive, uphold, and recite this sutra.
At that time, Ānanda spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"One should travel even a yojana, Or even as far as a hundred yojanas,
To hear and receive such a sutra as this, Which enables one to relinquish all fruits."
Even if there were a great pit of fire, a yojana in length and breadth,
a wise person would go through it to hear and receive such a sutra as this.
If one wishes to obtain the noble precepts, the most supreme among all precepts;
One should circulate this sutra, for it can purify the aggregate of ethical discipline.
Those who wish to attain the meditations of the noble ones— the most supreme among all meditations—
should circulate this sutra, which burns away all afflictions.
Those who wish to attain the wisdom of all the sages, the supreme among all forms of wisdom;
who should cause this sutra to circulate, for it can purify all dharma-realms;
and those who wish to travel to all directions to adorn and purify all worlds—[should uphold this sutra].
In the realm named Joy and Bliss, this sutra should be circulated.
Those who wish to see the Buddha Akṣobhya, the most honored among all Munis,
should uphold this sutra and expound it extensively for the sake of sentient beings.
If one wishes to purify the various practices of a bodhisattva,
One should circulate this sutra, And shall attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
There one shall behold Amitābha Buddha, Whose radiance is inconceivable.
"You should circulate this sutra, which has been spoken by all the Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
It is as you have said. Why is this?

If a son or daughter of good family recites and explains this sutra to others with an undistracted mind, they shall see all the Buddhas whenever they wish to see them; even if one recites and explains this sutra to others with a distracted mind, at the time of their death, that person will see hundreds of thousands of Buddhas with their own eyes.
"Why is this? Because all Buddhas protect these good men and good women.

At that time, there was a young girl in the assembly named Siṃhā, who, together with five hundred other girls, rose from her seat, bared her right shoulder, knelt with her right knee on the ground, joined her palms with single-minded devotion, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there is a woman who receives, maintains, reads, recites, and masters this sutra, what merit will she have?
At that time, the World-Honored One told Siṃha:
“If there is a woman who seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and receives, maintains, reads, recites, and masters this sutra, you should know that this body shall be her very last.”
Why is this? If there is a woman who, with an undistracted mind, upholds, recites, and masters this sutra, all afflictions that cause her to receive a female body will no longer manifest before her.
The Lion addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What afflictions cause one to receive a female body?"
The Buddha told Siṃha:
